v: But they, when they heard this, were cut to the heart, and were determined to kill them.
But one stood up in the council, a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, honored by all the people, and commanded to put the apostles out for a little while.
He said to them, “You men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do.

For before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves. He was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed, and came to nothing.
After this man, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, and drew away some people after him. He also perished, and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered abroad.
Now I tell you, withdraw from these men, and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown.
But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!”
They agreed with him. Summoning the apostles, they beat them and commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name.
Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ.
b: In the last devotion, the apostles preached a four-verse sermon before the Sanhedrin: obey God rather than men; you killed Him, but God raised Him; God exalted Him as Prince and Savior. The words were finished, and now we see how the Sanhedrin responded.

Chapter 5 begins with a couple falling dead at the apostles’ feet and ends with a group of men who have been beaten yet are rejoicing in their hearts. In this last passage, Luke has us see two reactions to the same sermon, and also see this: when people block what comes from God, the one they end up blocking is themselves.
I. “Cut to the heart, and determined to kill them”—One Sermon, Two Kinds of Hearts

In verse 33, the phrase “cut to the heart” literally means “sawn through,” as if a saw were cutting the heart open. Acts uses this word only twice. The other time is after Stephen’s sermon, when the crowd was “cut to the heart” and then stoned him to death (Acts 7:54). Interestingly, on the day of Pentecost, when Peter preached, the people were “cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37)—their hearts were pierced as well—but that time three thousand repented. The same Peter, the same message—“you killed Him, but God raised Him”—and one group asked, “What shall we do?” while another wanted to kill the preacher.

The difference lies not in the message but in the heart. When God’s word meets a heart willing to lay itself down, it becomes repentance; when it meets a heart clinging to self, it becomes rage. It is the same with us when we listen to preaching today: when a problem is pointed out, do we bow our heads and ask, “What shall I do?” or does a fire flare up inside, wanting to prove the speaker wrong? That fire is the evidence of self.
• One sermon, two outcomes: the difference lies in whether the hearer is willing to lay down self.
• The first reaction when a problem is pointed out: bowing the head to ask the way, or flaring up first?
II. “A Pharisee named Gamaliel”—God Has Someone Even in the Enemy’s Camp

Verses 34 and 35. Just as the Sanhedrin was seething with murderous intent, one man stood up: Gamaliel, a Pharisee, “a teacher of the law, honored by all the people.” He commanded that the apostles be put outside for a little while, then urged the council, “Take heed to yourselves what you are about to do.”

Gamaliel was the grandson of the rabbi Hillel and the first in Jewish tradition to be honored with the title “Rabban” (“our teacher”). He was a Pharisee—Pharisees believed in resurrection and angels, which the Sadducees denied on both counts, so the two parties were naturally opposed in the Sanhedrin. More importantly, he had a student named Saul, who would later become Paul (Acts 22:3). At this moment Gamaliel spoke up for the apostles, and his student would one day become the greatest of the apostles. God’s hand is in unexpected places.

Most in the Sanhedrin wanted to kill the apostles, yet God had placed one man there. The apostles did not defend themselves or look for someone to smooth things over; they simply preached and then stood still, and the one who spoke for them was prepared by God. One who is emptied of self does not need to scheme for himself, because God is the One scheming on his behalf.
• God has people even in the enemy’s camp: you need not scheme for yourself; He will prepare them.
III. “Theudas… Judas of Galilee”—What Is of Men, All Who Follow Scatter

Verses 36 and 37. Gamaliel cited two examples. Theudas boasted himself to be somebody, and about four hundred men joined him; when he was slain, all who followed him were dispersed. Judas of Galilee rose up “in the days of the enrollment”—that is, in AD 6, when Rome registered the Jewish land for taxation—and led people in revolt, and he also perished. This Judas was the source of the later Zealot movement.

Gamaliel’s observation was sharp: these movements had one thing in common—when the leader died, the people scattered. They were “of men”; the center was one man, and when he was gone, the center was gone. But the apostles’ movement was different: their Leader had been put to death, and the followers not only did not scatter but increased all the more. Gamaliel did not state this conclusion, but Luke places it here for the reader to see.

“Boasting himself to be somebody”—this was Theudas’s problem, and it is the root disease of everything that comes from men. Pride is leaving one’s place and wanting to take God’s; whatever is centered on man, however lively it is at the start, comes to nothing in the end. Turn the question on yourself: in what I am devoted to, is the center the Lord, or me? If I were gone one day, would it scatter, or would it go on?
• What is of men scatters when the man leaves: the center is a man, and when he is gone, the center is gone.
• Examine what you are devoted to: if I were gone, would it scatter, or continue?
IV. “If it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it”—The Wisdom and the Limits of the Neutral

Verses 38 and 39, Gamaliel’s conclusion: what is of men will come to nothing; what is of God you cannot overthrow, “lest perhaps you be found even to be fighting against God.” This sentence holds real wisdom: what comes from God, men cannot destroy; and in blocking what is from God, the one finally blocked is oneself. The empires that persecuted the church have passed away, and the church remains.

But we must also see Gamaliel’s limits. His principle is not entirely reliable—what is of men sometimes flourishes for a long time, and what is of God sometimes looks like failure; the cross is the clearest example. And his stance was “wait and see”: like a man standing at the window looking at the weather to decide whether to go out; he would not go out into the rain, nor would he say it would not rain today. Gamaliel saved the apostles’ lives but did not follow the apostles’ Lord. He recognized that this might be of God, yet did not give himself over.
Gamaliel came to the door, but stopped at the door. Recognizing God’s work and giving yourself to God are two different things.
• Don’t stop at the door: recognizing God’s work is not the same as giving yourself to Him.
V. “Rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name”—The End of Chapter 5

Verses 40 to 42. After hearing Gamaliel, the council still “beat them”—by the law, the scourging was at most forty lashes less one (Deut. 25:3; 2 Cor. 11:24)—and commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

The apostles left the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name.” With blood on their backs, they rejoiced in their hearts, and the reason was: they were counted worthy. The word “worthy” means “regarded as qualified.” They took suffering shame for the Lord as a qualification conferred by the Lord Himself. This is exactly what the Lord had said: “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you… Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad” (Matt. 5:11–12).

Jesus is my example—He first suffered dishonor for this Name, and now the disciples are counted worthy to share in that dishonor. Giving thanks in everything does not mean being able to say “thank you”; it means truly rejoicing in the heart while the back still hurts. That kind of joy belongs only to those whose focus is entirely on Jesus. If the focus is on self, being beaten is an injustice; if the focus is on Him, being beaten is being counted worthy.

Verse 42 is the last sentence of chapter 5. The council commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and their response was: every day, without ceasing, in the temple and from house to house, to teach and preach Jesus as the Christ. Persecution did not beat them small; it beat them more single-hearted.
• Counted worthy: suffering dishonor for this Name is a qualification given by the Lord, not an injustice.
• Every day, without ceasing: persecution cannot make small a people whose focus is on Jesus; it only makes them more single-hearted.
The Light of the 321 Principles: What Is of God Cannot Be Overthrown; Suffering Dishonor for the Name Is Being Counted Worthy

Chapter 5 traveled a long road: it began with Ananias and Sapphira falling at the apostles’ feet, passed through the shadow falling on the sick and the prison doors opened at night, and ended with a group of men with blood on their backs going out rejoicing and continuing to preach Jesus as the Christ.

This chapter tells us that God’s system is “of God.” It is not an idea a group of people thought up, nor a movement held up by one leader; when the Leader was killed, it did not scatter; when the apostles were beaten, it did not stop. What we build today, if the Lord is its center, has this kind of life; if self is its center, however lively it is, it will come to nothing.

And in this system, the individual’s appearance is “counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name.” The old self, living by self, finds shame the hardest thing to bear, because self wants face; the new self, emptied of self, finds that being able to suffer shame for that Name is a qualification. This is not self-consolation but a real change of focus: the focus is on Jesus, not on self, and everything suffered for Him becomes glory.
Gamaliel stopped at the door; the apostles went in. Chapter 5 ends between these two kinds of people and asks us: where do you stand?
a: Check Your First Reaction
When God’s word points out a problem, do you bow your head and ask the way, or flare up first?
Don’t Scheme for Yourself
The Lord will prepare people in unexpected places; just preach, then stand.
Ask Who the Center Is
In what you are devoted to, would it scatter if you were gone, or continue?
Don’t Stop at the Door
Recognize God’s work, and also give yourself to Him.
Count Shame as Qualification
Today, rewrite in your heart the hurt suffered for this Name as glory.
q: Gamaliel recognized that this “might be of God,” yet stopped at the door. Is there something in your life that you have already seen to be God’s work but have not yet given yourself into? What holds you back?

Recall the last time you suffered hurt for your faith—being misunderstood, looked down on, or excluded. Did your heart record it as “injustice” or as “worthy”? If you rewrote it as “counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name,” how would your heart be different?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that with the same sermon You caused three thousand to be cut to the heart and repent, and also caused the council to be enraged; the difference lies not in the message but in the heart. Thank You for preparing a Gamaliel even in the enemy’s camp, so that we know those emptied of self need not scheme for themselves.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often stand at the door like Gamaliel: recognizing Your work yet unwilling to give ourselves over; and we confess that we feel hurt at the least injustice, and seldom take suffering shame for You as a qualification You confer. Forgive us, and turn our focus from ourselves to You, that when problems are pointed out we bow our heads and ask the way, and when we are looked down upon we rejoice in our hearts. Search everything we are devoted to; if its center is ourselves, tear it down; if its center is You, establish it, so that no one can overthrow it. May we, like that group, every day, without ceasing, in the temple and from house to house, preach that You are the Christ. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service.
The twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables.
Therefore select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.”
These words pleased the whole multitude. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch;
whom they set before the apostles. When they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.
The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.
b: In the last devotion, the apostles were beaten before the Sanhedrin yet “departed rejoicing,” because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name; then every day in the temple and from house to house they ceaselessly taught and preached Jesus as the Christ. The whip from outside did not bring down the church; the more it was beaten, the more it flourished.

At the beginning of chapter 6, Luke turns the camera from the Sanhedrin back to the inside of the church. This time the crisis did not come from outside but rose from within—someone began to murmur. Satan could not break in from outside, so he took another road and worked from the inside. What we need to see is not only how they solved the problem, but what they put first as they solved it.
I. “The Hellenists murmured against the Hebrews”—The Crack That Growth Brings

“Hellenists” refers to Jews who had been scattered abroad and returned to settle in Jerusalem; they ordinarily spoke Greek and read the Old Testament in Greek. The “Hebrews” were the native-born Jews who spoke Aramaic. Both groups were Jews, both believed in Jesus, and both were in the same church, yet their language, culture, and habits differed.

The problem was in “the daily distribution”—the church gave out food to widows every day. The Greek-speaking widows were mostly returned expatriates, far from home with no relatives, those who most needed care, and it was exactly they who were “neglected.” The word “neglected” in the original does not mean deliberate exclusion but “overlooked”—no one meant harm; there were too few hands and the system had not kept up, so a group was left out.
• Growth itself brings cracks: with more people there are more corners no one sees; the problem is not growth but whether anyone is willing to bow down and look at that corner.
• Murmuring is a signal, not a charge: Luke does not rebuke the murmurers. When someone who has been wronged speaks up, that is exactly the voice the church should hear.
II. “It is not appropriate that we should forsake the word of God and serve tables”—First See Your Place Clearly
The Twelve responded maturely. They did not say, “Don’t fuss over small matters,” nor “Fine, we will go distribute the food ourselves.” They first asked a more basic question: where is our place?

The “serve” in “serve tables” in verse 2 and the “ministry” in “the ministry of the word” in verse 4 come from the same root in the original—both are “service.” So the apostles were not saying that distributing food is lowly—distributing food is service, and preaching is service. What they said was: if we do this service, we will “forsake” the word of God, and that is “not appropriate.” It is not that distributing food is bad, but that our place is not there.

Pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place. If the apostles had refused to let go even of the food distribution, they would have looked very diligent, but in reality they would have been unwilling to share authority, and the result would have been poor preaching and poor distribution too. True humility is knowing clearly where God has placed me, staying content there, and entrusting the rest to others with a calm heart.
• Let people be people: handing to others what is theirs to do honors God’s calling on them.

• Keeping your place is not laziness: what the apostles kept was the heaviest burden—prayer and the ministry of the word; they dared to keep it because they believed God would raise up others to keep the rest.
III. “Of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom”—Choose People by Life First
Among the three conditions in verse 3, not one is “capable,” “good with accounts,” or “well connected.” Distributing food was clearly a practical matter, yet the apostles looked at life first.

A good reputation is the testimony others can see; being full of the Holy Spirit is the reality inside; wisdom is applying that inner reality to specific matters. Of the three, the second is the root and the other two are fruit. This is exactly the order of “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” The church often reverses it: first looking at what a person can do, and only last asking about his relationship with God.

The seven names in verse 5 are all Greek names. That is, the church handed the responsibility and authority for the care to the very people of those who had been neglected. Not “we will distribute to you,” but “you take charge.” The group that had been left out now became the ones holding the keys.
• Life before ministry: even those who distribute food must be full of the Holy Spirit, because nothing in the church does not need the Spirit.
• Let the most wounded group hold the keys: what truly dissolves a divide is not explanation but trust.
IV. “When they had prayed, they laid their hands on them”—Service Is a Commission, Not a Chore

In the Old Testament, laying on hands is an act of “belonging and transfer”: in offerings, hands laid on the head of the sacrifice show that the sacrifice represents me; Moses laid hands on Joshua to show that authority and commission passed to him. The apostles’ laying on of hands turned the food distribution from “a miscellaneous task” into “a trust.” From that moment the seven were not volunteers but men sent.

In a family, if a child is merely “told to take out the trash,” he drags his feet; but if his father says earnestly, “From today, this part of the household is yours,” he takes out the trash quite differently. The difference lies not in the task but in the commission. Many services in the church become heavy and prompt complaint, often because they are only chores assigned from above, not prayed over and never made a trust.
• Pray first, then lay on hands: before hands do the work, place the matter and the person in God’s hands.
• Those entrusted have dignity: not “helping out,” but “being sent.”
V. “The word of God spread”—When the Inside Is Handled, the Outside Opens

Among the results in verse 7, the most surprising is “a great many of the priests were obedient to the faith.” The priests were the core of the temple system, the group hardest to change and with the most vested interests; the ones persecuting the church in earlier chapters were of the chief priests’ party. The church handled one internal problem of food distribution, and the gospel broke through to the hardest layer.

This was no accident. If there are cracks inside the church, outsiders see and do not believe; when the inside is united, the word of God spreads of itself. What Luke is saying is: these seven verses are not an administrative record but a record of revival. Revival does not begin with a big evangelistic campaign outside, but with a willingness to bow down inside and deal with one murmur.
• When the inside is open, the outside is open: unity is the channel through which the word of God spreads.
• Revival is the fruit of humility: God gives grace to the humble; for a group willing to share authority and trust people, God hands even the priests to them.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Return to Your Place and Let Jesus Be King
The key to this passage is one phrase: “It is not appropriate.”

The apostles were not unable to distribute food; they clearly knew it was not the place God had put them. The old self, living by self, loves to hold everything in its hands, because the more it grasps, the more it proves itself important; and the result of grasping everything is that nothing is done well, and then it complains about others. The new self, emptied of self, can calmly return to its place—what God has me do, I do wholeheartedly; what God has others do, I entrust to them with ease. This letting go is not shirking but letting Jesus be King: only if He is the Head does He have the right to decide where each member is.

Self-denial makes unity possible. If each person in the Jerusalem church had clung to his own authority, the crack between the two groups would only have deepened; once the apostles let go, the church trusted, and seven Greek names stood up, the crack was healed. This is building God’s system: not an organizational structure but a people who return to their place and let Jesus be King, each keeping his own portion, and in them the word of God spreads.
a: Hear the Voice from the Corner
In the church, at home, on the team—is there someone I have “overlooked”? Go and look today.
Return to Your Place
Ask yourself: where has God put me? Have I grasped what I should not, and dropped what I should not?
Life Before Ministry
Be filled with the Holy Spirit, then go and work; not work first and add life later.
Dissolve Divides with Trust
To the one who differs from me, don’t explain—hand him the keys.
Begin from the Inside
Don’t seek revival outside; first deal with the unspoken murmur inside yourself.
q: In your service or work, is there something that is actually not the place God gave you, yet you keep gripping it? If you let it go, what do you fear losing most?

The apostles handed the care and authority to the very people of those who had been neglected. Is there someone near you who differs from you whom you still cannot trust with responsibility? How does God want you to trust him?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that the whip from outside did not bring down the church, and that You did not let the murmuring inside tear it apart. Thank You for showing us that the early apostles, facing a crack, neither panicked nor suppressed, but returned to their place, shared the service, and looked first at life, then at ministry. Your word spread in such humility, and even the priests became obedient.
Lord, we confess that we often want to hold everything in our hands, thinking the more we grasp the more important we are, and then nothing is done well and we blame others. Take away the “self” within us that leaves its place and grasps power; teach us to know clearly where You have placed us, to keep that portion wholeheartedly, and to entrust the rest with ease. Open our eyes to see the overlooked corners, make our hearts willing to trust those who differ from us, and let our churches and our homes become, through unity, places where Your word spreads. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Stephen, full of faith and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.
But some of those who were of the synagogue called “The Libertines”, and of the Cyrenians, of the Alexandrians, and of those of Cilicia and Asia arose, disputing with Stephen.
They weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke.
Then they secretly induced men to say, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.”
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, and came against him and seized him, then brought him in to the council,
and set up false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law.
For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place, and will change the customs which Moses delivered to us.”
All who sat in the council, fastening their eyes on him, saw his face like it was the face of an angel.
b: In the last devotion, the church chose seven men to oversee the food distribution, the apostles laid hands on them, and the word of God spread. The first of the seven names was Stephen—Luke specially notes that he was “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit.”

Now the camera stays on him. This man chosen to distribute food did not stay beside the table. He did great wonders among the people, debated in the synagogues, and was finally dragged before the council. From 6:8 to 7:60, Luke gives a whole chapter and a half to Stephen—longer than Peter’s sermon at Pentecost. For Stephen was not only the first martyr; he was the key that pushed the gospel out of Jerusalem and out of the temple. Today’s passage is the account of his being accused; the seventh chapter, beginning tomorrow, is his defense.
I. “Full of grace and power”—The Food Distributor Became a Worker of Miracles

Verse 8 says Stephen, “full of faith and power,” did great wonders and signs among the people. Until now in Acts, those who did miracles were apostles; Stephen is the first non-apostle to do miracles.

This shows one thing: God’s power does not follow titles; it follows life. Stephen was chosen because he was “full of the Holy Spirit”; he could do miracles also because he was full of the Holy Spirit. Distributing food and doing miracles were not two ranks in him but two things flowing from the same source. The word “full” in the original means “filled to overflowing”—he was first filled, and then it overflowed.
• Gifts follow life: not first seeking position and then power, but first being filled, and power overflows naturally.
• Those faithful in small things, God gives great things: he was first willing to oversee food, and then God had him do wonders among the people.
II. “Those of the synagogue of the Freedmen… rose up, disputing with Stephen”—Opposition Often Comes from Those Most Like You

Verse 9 lists the names of several synagogues. “Freedmen” (Libertines) transliterates the Latin for “freed men,” referring to Jews who had once been taken captive as slaves and later freed, and their descendants; Cyrene is in North Africa, Alexandria in Egypt, Cilicia and Asia in today’s Turkey. These are synagogues built by Jews scattered abroad who returned to Jerusalem—that is, they were exactly the “Hellenists.”

Stephen himself was a Hellenist. Those who rose to dispute with him were not the native Hebrew party but his own countrymen, his own circle. This is very common and very painful: the fiercest opposition often comes not from the farthest, but from those most like you and who know you best. Incidentally, the capital of Cilicia was Tarsus, and a young man of Tarsus named Saul was quite possibly sitting in that synagogue.
• Don’t be surprised by the source of opposition: the Lord Himself “came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him” (John 1:11).
• The focus is not on who opposes: it is on Jesus—not on self, not on others, not on circumstances.
III. “They weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke”—The Eloquence the Lord Promised
Verse 10 says, “They weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke.”

This almost fulfills the Lord’s promise word for word: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to withstand or to contradict” (Luke 21:15). Stephen did not overcome people by rhetorical skill; he spoke by the Holy Spirit. “Wisdom” here is not cleverness but knowing when to say what, and how to apply God’s word to the situation at hand.

A person who debates relying on his own mind grows more anxious the longer he argues, because he wants to win; a person who speaks by the Holy Spirit is not anxious, because he is not contending for himself. Using the mind and relying on self brings worry; using the heart and relying on the Spirit brings joy. What the crowd “couldn’t withstand” was not Stephen’s eloquence but the One behind him.
• Before speaking, ask who is speaking: is it my self that wants to win, or the Holy Spirit who wants to speak through me?
• What cannot be withstood is not a person: a person can be refuted; the Holy Spirit cannot.
IV. “Blasphemous words against Moses and God” “Against this holy place and the law”—Half a True Word Hidden in the Slander

Unable to out-argue him, they changed tactics. Verse 11, “they secretly induced men,” means bribing and instigating; in verse 12 they “stirred up” the people, the elders, and the scribes—exactly the three groups that made up the council; in verse 13 they “set up false witnesses.” The whole process was almost the same as the Lord Jesus’ trial a few months earlier.

The accusation had two charges: speaking against “this holy place” and “the law,” that is, the temple and Moses. Verse 14 is more specific: this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs Moses delivered. This was false witness, but the most powerful thing about false witness is that it holds half a true word—the Lord did say, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), and Stephen quite probably also taught that God’s presence is not limited to this temple, and that Jesus is the prophet greater than Moses.

The method of false witness is to twist true words into crimes. Stephen said God is greater than the temple, and they said he spoke against the temple; Stephen said Jesus fulfills the law, and they said he would change the law.
• Being misunderstood is part of following the Lord: as the Lord was twisted, so will His servants be.
• Remember these two charges: the temple and Moses are exactly the two topics Stephen’s whole defense in chapter 7 will answer.
V. “His face was like the face of an angel”—Besieged, Light on His Face
Verse 15 is the most beautiful sentence in this passage. All who sat in the council “looked intently at him” and saw that his face was “like the face of an angel.”

Luke does not explain what that looked like, but everyone familiar with the Old Testament would think of Moses: when he came down from Mount Sinai, “he didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him” (Exod. 34:29). They accused Stephen of blaspheming Moses, yet at this moment Stephen’s face shone like Moses’ face. God Himself bore witness for him.

A west-facing window at dusk is filled with the glow of sunset—not because the window shines by itself but because it faces the setting sun. A person’s face is like this: what a person often gazes at is what is reflected on his face. In the council Stephen did not look at that crowd gnashing their teeth; he looked at the Lord, so what his face reflected was light from heaven. Self-denial is not a slogan but a face that is besieged yet without fear or resentment.
• The face reflects the direction you look: looking at people reflects anxiety; looking at the Lord reflects glory.
• God bears witness for His servants: the false witness men give cannot cover the true witness God gives on his face.
The Light of the 321 Principles: One Filled with the Holy Spirit Cannot Be Withstood, Twisted, or Frightened

In the story of Stephen, Luke uses three angles to say the same thing: he spoke by the Holy Spirit and the crowd could not withstand him; he was twisted by false witnesses but did not strike back; he was dragged before the council, yet his face was like an angel’s.

All three point to one root: he was full of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is my guide—not only guiding in smooth times, but also when being debated, falsely accused, and besieged. The old self, living by self, has three reactions in these three situations: in debate it wants to win, under false accusation it wants to defend itself, under siege it is afraid. The center of all three reactions is “me.” The new self, emptied of self, can let the Holy Spirit speak in debate, quietly entrust itself under false accusation, and fix its eyes on the Lord under siege. This is not good self-cultivation but letting Jesus be King—when the King sits within, the face can have that kind of light.
And the end of this road is that Jesus receives all the glory. No one credited that shining face to Stephen; everyone saw God.
a: Be Filled First
Don’t seek power for great things; first be filled with the Holy Spirit in small things like distributing food.
Don’t Be Surprised by Opposition
When those most like you oppose you, withdraw your focus from them and put it back on the Lord.
Let the Holy Spirit Speak
Before opening your mouth to argue, ask: is it my self that wants to win, or does the Lord want to speak through me?
Accept Being Twisted
When a true word is twisted into a crime, don’t rush to defend yourself; place it in the Lord’s hands.
Fix Your Eyes on the Lord
In a besieging situation today, practice not looking at people but at the Lord, and let your face reflect His light.
q: The last time you were misunderstood or twisted by someone, was your first reaction to defend, strike back, or quietly entrust? What does that reaction show about whom you were fixing your eyes on?
Stephen was faithful beside the table first, and then God had him do wonders among the people. Is there a “small thing” in your hands right now that God is using to fill you and prepare you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You made a man chosen to distribute food full of grace and power; a man besieged by his own countrymen You gave wisdom and the Holy Spirit so that the crowd could not withstand him; a man falsely accused by false witnesses and dragged before the council, You made his face like the face of an angel. Thank You for showing us that a life filled with the Holy Spirit cannot be withstood, cannot be twisted, and cannot be frightened.
Lord, we confess that in debate we always want to win, in misunderstanding we always rush to defend ourselves, and under siege we are always afraid first. Take away the “self” within us that centers everything on itself, so that in every situation we let the Holy Spirit guide and let You be King. Teach us to fix our eyes on You and not on those faces gnashing their teeth; and in the hardest moments let our faces reflect Your light, so that what people see is not us but You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The high priest said, “Are these things so?”
He said, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran,
and said to him, ‘Get out of your land and away from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you.’
Then he came out of the land of the Chaldaeans and lived in Haran. From there, when his father was dead, God moved him into this land, where you are now living.
He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on. He promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his offspring after him, when he still had no child.
God spoke in this way: that his offspring would live as aliens in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.
‘I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage,’ said God, ‘and after that they will come out, and serve me in this place.’

He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs.
b: In the last devotion, Stephen was accused by false witnesses of “speaking against this holy place and the law,” and those in the council looked intently at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel. The high priest spoke: “Are these things so?”

Stephen’s answer is the longest sermon in Acts. Strangely, he did not say, “I never said that,” nor did he defend himself. He began with Abraham and told the history of Israel from the beginning. This was not a digression but the deepest defense: you say I speak against the temple and Moses, so let us return to the Scriptures and see what kind of God God really is, and how your ancestors treated those He sent. The whole sermon has two main threads: God has never been limited to one place or one temple; and Israel again and again rejected those God sent. Today’s eight verses are the beginning of the first thread.
I. “Brothers and fathers, listen”—The Defense Begins with Respect

Facing a council about to condemn him to death, Stephen’s first words were “Brothers and fathers, listen.” “Fathers” is the respectful title for elders and the high priest; “brothers” places himself with them in the same people. He did not treat the council as enemies; he treated them as fellow countrymen.

This matters. What Stephen was about to say was extremely sharp, but his starting point was not hatred; it was one in the same family urging his family. A person with self in his heart, when falsely accused, will first of all draw a line: you are you and I am I. One emptied of self can still say “brothers and fathers” when accused—because what he wants is not to escape himself but for these people to turn back.
• Respect is not weakness: truth can be spoken very heavily while the manner remains very respectful.
• Relationship before right and wrong: people matter more than the case; he cared about these “brothers and fathers,” not only this lawsuit.
II. “In Mesopotamia… the God of glory appeared”—God Appeared Outside the Promised Land
The first thing Stephen said went straight to the core of the accusation. He said: the God of glory appeared to Abraham “when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.”

Mesopotamia is the land between two rivers, around today’s Iraq, the land of the Chaldeans who worshiped the moon god. At that time there was no promised land, no temple, no law, not even the nation of Israel. “The God of glory”—a title often linked in the Old Testament with the glory in the temple—appeared in a foreign land a thousand miles away.

This sentence is as good as saying: you think God’s glory dwells in this temple, but the first time God appeared to our ancestors, it was a thousand kilometers from this temple. God has never been confined by one piece of land or one temple; wherever He wants to appear, He appears. You who accuse me of speaking against the temple—it is you who have made God small.
• God is greater than His temple: He can meet people in the temple and He can meet people in Chaldea; He can meet you in the church, and also on a sickbed or in an office.
• Calling comes before everything: Abraham first heard God, and only then came land, people, and temple. The order is first God, then the rest.
III. “Not even a foot’s length”—A Person of Faith Sojourns All His Life

Verse 5 is the most striking line in this passage: when Abraham came to the promised land, God “gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on.” In his whole life he bought only one burial plot. The promise was real, yet he never held it in his hand until he died, “when he still had no child.”

The ancestors of Israel were strangers on this earth. Hebrews says they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb. 11:13). Stephen wanted the council to see clearly: this land, this temple that you cling to so tightly—your ancestors never owned one inch of it; all he owned was God’s promise.

Someone staying in a hotel does not knock down the walls to redecorate, because he knows he checks out tomorrow; he carries only what matters most on his person. Abraham lived like this—what he carried with him was God’s word. People with self buy property frantically in the land of sojourning, treating the temporary as eternal; people emptied of self turn earth into heaven and the temporary into the eternal, and when the hands loosen, the heart is free.
• The promise is more reliable than property: to hold not an inch of land yet have one word from God is enough.
• The sojourner’s mindset: the one thing you grip hardest today—if you had to “check out” tomorrow, could you take it with you?
IV. “Four hundred years” “Serve me in this place”—God’s Plan Is Longer Than Human Sight

In verses 6 and 7, God told Abraham: your descendants will sojourn in a foreign land, be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years; then I will judge that nation, and they will come out and “serve me in this place.”

Abraham did not yet have even a son, and God had already told him what would happen four hundred years later. In those four hundred years there would be Egypt, slavery, the exodus, the wilderness—all on God’s schedule. When Israel suffered in Egypt they may have thought God had forgotten; actually He had said it four hundred years earlier.

In the phrase “serve me in this place,” the weight in the original is on “serve,” not on “this place.” God’s purpose in bringing them out was that they might serve Him, not that they might possess a piece of land. The land is for serving; serving is not for the land. The council had reversed the order: they guarded the land and the temple, yet no longer served the God who gave the land and the temple.
• Suffering is in God’s plan: the “Egypt” you are in today is not an accident of God’s plan but a stretch He had already counted in.
• The purpose is serving, not possessing: whatever God gives you, it is so that you may use it to serve Him.
V. “The covenant of circumcision”—The Sign Is on the Body, Not on the Land
In verse 8, God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and then Isaac, Jacob, and the twelve patriarchs were born in succession.

Circumcision is the sign of the covenant, cut into a person’s body, not into the land. Stephen will use this at the end: he will accuse the council of being “uncircumcised in heart and ears” (7:51). The true sign is of the heart; outward circumcision without inward reality is only a surgery.

This verse also closes the passage on “the twelve patriarchs”—and the first sentence of the next passage (7:9) is “the patriarchs, becoming jealous of Joseph.” No sooner was God’s covenant established than the heirs of the covenant went wrong. This is the beginning of the second thread: the people of God’s covenant again and again rejected those God sent.
• The covenant is set on the body, not on the land: wherever you are, God’s covenant goes with you.
• The sign needs reality: those who received the sign can also be jealous and reject; the sign cannot save, only returning to a relationship with God.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Where God Is, Your Place Is
Stephen began with Abraham, but he was really saying one thing: God is greater than any piece of land, any temple, any system; those who follow Him sojourn all their lives within His calling.

The old self, living by self, needs something to grasp—land, temple, position, achievement—because those things make “me” feel secure and important. The council grasped the temple; what we grasp may be the size of a ministry, church tradition, our own seniority. Yet when God appeared to Abraham, He gave him nothing, only a word and a promise. This is the starting point of “the Bible is my standard”: not living by what is seen and owned, but living by what God has said.

Self-denial is not having nothing, but entering the limitless. Abraham had not even a foot of ground, yet became the father of many nations; what he loosened was a piece of land, and what he gained was God Himself. Those who let Jesus be King need not first own anything in order to serve Him—wherever He appears is holy ground; wherever He calls you is your place.
a: Speak Truth with Respect
To those who oppose you, still say “brothers and fathers”; relationship before right and wrong.
Don’t Make God Small
God meets you in the church, and also in the least spiritual corner of your life.
Learn to Be a Pilgrim
Today loosen the one thing you grip hardest; practice seeing the temporary as temporary.
Trust God’s Schedule
The “four hundred years” you are going through were already in His plan.
Check the Sign in Your Heart
All the outward signs of faith are in place—but is there still jealousy and rejection inside?
q: When God appeared to Abraham, He gave him nothing, only a word. If God gave you only a word today, with no visible assurance, would you rise and follow? What holds you back?
In your life, what is it that you “thought God’s glory dwells only there”—a way of serving, a place, a tradition? Is God now wanting you to see that He is greater than that?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the God of glory yet do not dwell in temples made by human hands; You appeared to Abraham in Chaldea, watched over Your people in Egypt, and meet us in the least spiritual corners of our lives. Thank You for showing us that You are never limited to one place or one temple, and that Your calling is our place for all our lives.
Lord, we confess that we often, like the council, grasp a piece of land, a system, an achievement, thinking that is Your presence; and we forget that Abraham had not even a foot of ground and lived only by Your word. Take away the “self” within us that needs to grasp things to feel secure; teach us to be pilgrims, to see the temporary as temporary, and to take Your word as our only inheritance. Search the sign in our hearts, that we may have not only outward ritual but also real obedience within. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt. God was with him,
and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house.
Now a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. Our fathers found no food.
But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time.
On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s race was revealed to Pharaoh.
Joseph sent and summoned Jacob, his father, and all his relatives, seventy-five souls.
Jacob went down into Egypt and he died, himself and our fathers,
and they were brought back to Shechem, and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver from the children of Hamor of Shechem.
b: In the last devotion, Stephen began with Abraham: the God of glory appeared to him in Mesopotamia, yet in the promised land gave him not even a foot of ground; God made with him the covenant of circumcision, and the line continued to the twelve patriarchs. No sooner was the covenant established than the first sentence of verse 9 says: “The patriarchs, becoming jealous of Joseph.”

This is the beginning of the second main thread of the whole sermon—the one God sent to save was first rejected by his own brothers. When Stephen told it through Joseph, the council would not at first find it jarring, because it was a story they knew perfectly well. But every detail Stephen chose was laying a road leading to that last sentence, “As your fathers did, so do you.”
I. “The patriarchs, becoming jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt”—The First Rejection

Stephen did not call them “Joseph’s older brothers”; he said “the patriarchs”—the “twelve patriarchs” of verse 8, the ancestors of whom everyone in the council was proud. The first thing recorded of them was jealousy, and then selling their brother.

The word “jealous” in the original means “to be hot”—seeing their younger brother favored by their father, and dreaming that he would be king, burned them inside. Jealousy is the garment pride most often wears: I cannot bear that God chose him and not me. In an office, when the youngest colleague is appreciated by the boss, the others say congratulations with their mouths while in their hearts they begin looking for his faults—that fire is the same fire that was in Joseph’s brothers.

And the one God chose was pushed out in exactly this way by his own brothers. Joseph’s being sold was the first time Israel rejected the one God sent; later there was Moses, then the prophets, and finally the Righteous One. Stephen was laying out this line layer by layer.
• Jealousy is the body temperature of pride: when your heart grows “hot” at someone’s success, examine your self.
• Rejecting those God sent often begins with those closest: Joseph was not sold by foreigners but by his brothers.
II. “But God was with him”—In Egypt, God Was There Too

The second half of verse 9 is only five words, yet it is the turning point of the whole passage: “But God was with him.” Joseph was sold into Egypt—far from the promised land, far from his father’s house, far from everything that could be called “holy”—yet God was with him there, delivered him out of all his afflictions, gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, and made him governor.

This returns to the first thread: God is not limited to one place. The last devotion was Chaldea; this one is Egypt. The foreign land Israel most despised was exactly where God was with Joseph and exalted him. The council thought God’s presence was locked on Mount Zion; Stephen says God was with Joseph in prison and with him in Pharaoh’s court.

Notice the two things Joseph received: favor and wisdom. These are exactly the words used of Stephen in 6:8 and 6:10—“full of grace” and “spoke with wisdom and the Spirit.” Luke wants us to see: what Stephen was telling was what he himself was living. He too was pushed by his own brothers to the council, and God was with him too.
• God’s presence follows the person, not the land: the “Egypt” you are pushed into—God is already there before you.
• Suffering is not proof of being abandoned: every day Joseph was in prison God was with him, though he could not see it then.
III. “The second time Joseph was made known to his brothers”—The First Time They Did Not Recognize Him; the Second Time They Did

Verses 11 to 14 tell of the famine. Jacob sent his sons to Egypt “the first time”; that time they stood before Joseph and did not recognize him; “the second time” Joseph was made known to his brothers, and the whole family of seventy-five came down to Egypt.

“The first time” and “the second time”—Stephen deliberately marks them. The first time, the deliverer stood before them and they did not know him; the second time they recognized that the brother they had sold was the one who preserved their lives. When he comes to Moses, Stephen will use the same structure again: Moses first went to visit his brothers and was pushed away; forty years later the second time he was accepted.
If those in the council understood, they would tremble: that Nazarene whom you nailed to the cross is your brother, whom you did not recognize the first time. He will have a second time.
• Rejection is not the end: those not recognized the first time, God gives a second chance; the question is whether your heart is ready when the second time comes.
• The key to recognizing Him is famine: the brothers came to Joseph only when the grain ran out. People often know the Lord only in lack.
IV. “They died there… buried in Shechem”—What the Ancestors Owned Was a Tomb

Verses 15 and 16: Jacob and our fathers died in Egypt, their bodies were carried back and laid in the tomb Abraham bought for a sum of silver. Stephen compresses the two land purchases into one sentence; his point is not the details but the conclusion: what the ancestors owned in the promised land was only a bought tomb.

And that tomb was in Shechem—the council would frown at that name, because Shechem was in Samaria, the place they despised most. Stephen was in effect saying: even the burial place of your ancestors is in Samaria. God’s promise never depended on a piece of land; the ancestors died one after another outside the promise, yet died one after another in faith (Heb. 11:13).
A person who places a lifetime’s hope on visible property leaves behind in the end only a tomb; one who places hope on God’s promise finds the tomb only a temporary inn, not the end.
• See what you are storing up: of all you grip, how many things can you take into the tomb?
• To die in faith is also to live in faith: the ancestors did not see the promise fulfilled, yet not one gave up the promise.
The Light of the 321 Principles: For One Rejected by His Brothers, God Is with Him
Stephen used only eight verses on Joseph’s story, but both threads are in it: his brothers were jealous of him and sold him; yet God was with him and exalted him.

The old self, living by self, shows itself most typically in jealousy—unable to bear that God chooses and exalts someone else, and so trying to push that person out. And the one pushed out, if self is also in his heart, responds with resentment; Joseph did not. In Egypt he had not one word of complaint; he fixed his focus on God, so God could be with him in Egypt. The focus is on Jesus, not on self, not on others, not on circumstances—this is exactly why Joseph could live out the same life in prison and in the palace.

Jesus is my example, and Joseph is a shadow of Jesus: sold by his brothers, yet becoming his brothers’ salvation; not recognized the first time, acknowledged the second. Those who follow the Lord must walk this road too—misunderstood and pushed away by their own, yet not responding with self, only letting God be with us. Such a person, when “the second time” comes, will become a place where others receive grain.
a: Check the Heat in Your Heart
Toward whose success is your heart “hot”? That is jealousy, the body temperature of pride.
Trust God in Your Egypt
The place you are pushed to—God is already there waiting for you.
Don’t Answer Rejection with Resentment
Like Joseph, withdraw your focus from those who sold you and put it back on God.
Prepare for the Second Time
The person or matter you did not recognize or accept the first time—if God gives a second chance, is your heart ready?
Count Your Property
Of what you grip hardest today, how many things can a tomb carry away?
q: Think honestly: lately is there someone, because God has exalted him, toward whom your heart grows “hot”? What do you intend to do with that fire?
Joseph had not one word of complaint in Egypt. In the “place you did not choose” where you are now, are you counting the injuries of rejection, or looking for evidence that God is with you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that when Joseph was sold into Egypt by his own brothers, You were with him; in prison You were with him; before Pharaoh You gave him favor and wisdom. Thank You for showing us that Your presence is not limited to one piece of land; wherever we are pushed, You are already there.
Lord, we confess that in our hearts too is the fire of Joseph’s brothers—growing hot when we see You exalt others, wanting to push away those You choose. Take away the “self” within us that cannot bear others being exalted, so that we can truly rejoice in our brothers’ blessing. And when we are misunderstood and pushed away, keep us from answering with resentment, and fix our focus on You; make our “Egypt” a place where others receive grain, and let the place where we did not recognize You the first time be where we recognize You the second. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “But as the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until there arose a different king, who didn’t know Joseph.
The same took advantage of our race, and mistreated our fathers, and forced them to throw out their babies, so that they wouldn’t stay alive.
At that time Moses was born, and was exceedingly handsome. He was nourished three months in his father’s house.
When he was thrown out, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and reared him as her own son.
Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.
But when he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel.
Seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and avenged him who was oppressed, striking the Egyptian.
He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they didn’t understand.
“The day following, he appeared to them as they fought, and urged them to be at peace again, saying, ‘Sirs, you are brothers. Why do you wrong one another?’
But he who did his neighbor wrong pushed him away, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?
Do you want to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’
Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.
b: In the last devotion, Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers, yet God was with him; the brothers did not recognize him the first time and knew him only the second; in the end the fathers all died in Egypt, owning only a tomb in the Promised Land.

Now Stephen comes to Moses. This is the longest section of the whole sermon (7:17–43), because the council had accused him of speaking blasphemy against Moses, so he sets out to tell Moses’ life plainly, to show who was really despising Moses. Today’s thirteen verses cover Moses’ first forty years: how he was born, how he grew up, how he first went out to visit his brothers, and how his brothers pushed him away.
I. “As the time of the promise drew near”—When God’s Time Came, So Did the Persecution

Verse 17 says that as the time of the promise drew near, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt; verse 18 follows at once: another king arose who did not know Joseph. As the promise drew near, suffering reached its height—the new king dealt craftily with the people and forced them to expose their babies.

Stephen sets these two things side by side on purpose. God’s deliverance often begins in the deepest darkness, not after the darkness has lifted. In the days when Israel’s babies were being cast out, God’s promise may have felt farthest away; in truth it was nearest.

“A new king who did not know Joseph” is also a heavy phrase. Joseph saved the whole land of Egypt, and a generation later no one remembered. Human gratitude lasts only a few generations, but not one word of God’s promise falls to the ground.
• The darkest hour is the nearest hour: when God feels farthest today, it may be that the time of His promise is drawing near.
• People forget, God does not: do not rest your hope on whether people remember you, but on God remembering His promise.
II. “Beautiful before God… learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians”—God Prepares a Deliverer in the Enemy’s Palace

Verses 20–22 tell of Moses’ birth and education. “Beautiful before God,” as the original reads; his parents hid him for three months, then he was cast out by the river, and Pharaoh’s daughter took him and raised him as her own son. So the Hebrew baby who should have been killed grew up in the palace of the very king who sought to kill him, “instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.”

Here Stephen strikes his first main theme again: God is not bound to one place. God meant to rescue Israel, yet He had the deliverer raised in Pharaoh’s palace and equipped with the enemy’s own resources. He called Abraham in Mesopotamia, exalted Joseph in Egypt, and prepared Moses in Pharaoh’s house. Those who accused Stephen thought God worked only in the temple; Stephen shows again and again that God has always worked where you least expect.

• God uses what you think of as enemy ground to prepare you: the environment you least wanted to be in, the least spiritual training you received, may be where God is equipping you for a later calling.
• Don’t despise what seems “unlike what God would use”: the wisdom of Egypt later went into the writing of the Pentateuch.
III. “He supposed that his brothers would understand… but they did not understand”—The First Rejection

Verses 23–25: when Moses was nearly forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers. He saw one of them being wronged, defended him, and struck down the Egyptian. Verse 25 is the heart of the passage: “He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they did not understand.”

Notice the two “understands.” Moses supposed his brothers would understand; his brothers did not. Moses carried a burden for deliverance—a real burden, put there by God; but what he used was “his hand”—his own hand, his own timing, his own method. Moses at forty had learning, ability and zeal, but not God’s sending. He was the right man doing the right thing, at the wrong time and in the wrong way.

Picture someone eager to help who, while the owner is away, rearranges all the furniture in the house; the owner returns and, far from being grateful, is angry. It is not that the helper had a bad heart; it is that, as he worked, the center was “I feel it should be this way.” Using my head and relying on myself, the more zealous I am the more trouble I cause; using my heart and relying on the Holy Spirit, I will wait for God’s time.
• The burden is real, the method may be self: having God’s burden is not the same as having God’s sending.

• “His hand” and “God’s hand”: the same task is a disaster when I do it myself and a deliverance when God sends me. Forty years later God said, “Come now, and I will send you” (7:34)—that was God’s hand.
IV. “Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?”—The Words of Rejection

Verses 26–28: the next day Moses saw two Israelites fighting and urged them to be reconciled: “Men, you are brothers.” The one who was mistreating his neighbor pushed him away and spoke the most piercing words of the passage: “Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?”

Stephen wants the council to hear this sentence clearly, because in verse 35 he will say it again word for word. Israel rejected Moses by questioning his authority—who appointed you? And they rejected Jesus in exactly the same way: “By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?” (Matt. 21:23). Joseph was sold by his brothers, Moses was pushed away by his brothers; the line grows clearer and clearer.

What is more sorrowful is that this time Moses was not striking anyone; he was making peace—not contending for himself, but for harmony among brothers. And the one who pushed him away was “the one who did his neighbor wrong”—the wrong party. People reject those God sends not often because the messenger is wrong, but because his words touch their own wrong.
• Being questioned about authority is the common mark of those God sends: Joseph, Moses, the prophets and Jesus all walked this road.
• The one who pushes away the peacemaker is often the one doing wrong: when I badly want to push someone away, I should first ask whether I am the one “who did his neighbor wrong.”
V. “At this saying Moses fled”—Forty Years in the Wilderness
Verse 29: Moses fled and lived as a foreigner in Midian, where he had two sons. From prince to shepherd, from the learning of Egypt to the dust of the wilderness. Forty years.

Stephen covers it in one verse, but these forty years were the most important lesson of Moses’ life. At forty Moses had everything, except that he was too full—full of learning, full of ability, full of his own ideas; at eighty Moses had nothing, only a shepherd’s staff, and then God could use him. The wilderness is not punishment; it is emptying. God must empty out “his hand” before it can be replaced by “God’s hand.”
• The wilderness is the place of emptying: God brings you into the wilderness not because He doesn’t want you, but to pour out the self within you.
• God is not afraid to wait: He would rather wait forty years than use someone who still relies on himself.
The Light of the 321 Principles: From “His Hand” to “God’s Hand”
Moses’ first forty years were a lesson about self.

He had a burden from God, outstanding ability, and a heart willing to give himself for his brothers—all of it good. But verse 25 says he supposed God was delivering them “by his hand.” The self here is not an evil heart; it is the self inside a good heart: I know what to do, I will do it now, my brothers will surely understand. For the old self’s life of self, this is the hardest kind to detect: not proudly bullying others, but zealously doing God’s work for Him.

To make the Holy Spirit my guide means that even the timing and method of deliverance are not mine to set. It took Moses forty years of wilderness to learn to wait for God to say, “Come now, and I will send you.” Self-denial is not doing nothing, but not acting on one’s own; it is not having no burden, but handing the burden back to the God who gave it, waiting for His time and using His method. Such a person is one on whose hand God can lay His hand.
a: Count the Days in the Dark
When God feels farthest, practice believing that His promise is “drawing near.”
Don’t Despise Your Egypt
God may be equipping you through the very environment you least want to be in.
Tell Burden from Sending
When you have a burden, don’t act first; ask God whether it is now and whether it is this way.
Examine the Hand That Pushes
The person you badly want to push away—have they touched your wrong?
Accept the Wilderness
When God brings you into a season of emptying, don’t rush out; let Him pour out all your self.
q: Is there a “burden from God” you are about to carry out right now with “your own hand”? How do you tell whether it is God’s sending or the kind of zeal Moses had at forty?
Recall a time you were “pushed away” and a time you “pushed away” someone else. In the latter, were you the one “who did his neighbor wrong”? What does God want you to do about it?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in the darkest days, when Israel’s babies were being cast out, Your promise was drawing near; and that in Pharaoh’s palace You prepared a deliverer. Thank You for showing us that You are never limited by circumstances, that You work where we least expect, and that You equip us with things we thought useless.
Lord, we confess that we are often like Moses at forty: we have a burden, ability and zeal, yet we work for You with our own hands, and our brothers do not understand and things are spoiled. Take away the well-meaning “self” within us, teach us to tell burden from sending, and to wait until You say, “Come now, and I will send you.” Make us unafraid of the wilderness and willing to be emptied, so that Your hand may rest on our hands. Have mercy on us, that we may not be those who push away the peacemaker, but those who listen to the ones You send. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.
When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight. As he came close to see, a voice of the Lord came to him,
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ Moses trembled, and dared not look.
The Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground.
I have surely seen the affliction of my people that is in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you into Egypt.’
“This Moses, whom they refused, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—God has sent him as both a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This man led them out, having worked wonders and signs in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
b: In the last devotion, Moses at forty tried to deliver his brothers with his own hand, but they did not understand and pushed him away: “Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?” He fled to Midian, and was gone for forty years.

Today’s passage is the end of those forty years. An eighty-year-old shepherd sees in the wilderness a bush burning yet not consumed, and God speaks to him there. Every line of Stephen’s telling answers the council’s accusation: You say I speak against the holy place? Look—the first time God speaks of “holy ground” is in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, not in Jerusalem. You say I blaspheme Moses? Look—who rejected Moses, and who sent him?
I. “After forty years, in the wilderness of Mount Sinai”—God Appears in the Wilderness

Verse 30: after forty years. Moses at eighty was long past being the gifted prince; what he did every day was tend sheep. And in just such days, “an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.”

The place is “the wilderness of Mount Sinai.” This matters greatly to Stephen’s defense. He has already told how God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, and prepared Moses in Pharaoh’s house; now he says God appeared in a bush in the wilderness. Four times, never in the Promised Land, never in the temple. God seems to avoid the very places people think He must appear, so that people may know He is not a God invited into a building, but a God who appears wherever He wills.
• God’s chosen places are often surprising: not in the temple but in the wilderness; not on the peak you imagine but in the everyday you think has no spiritual value.
• Forty years of waiting was not wasted: Moses did not meet God in Pharaoh’s palace but in the wilderness where he tended sheep.
II. “I am the God of your fathers”—God First Says Who He Is
Verses 31–32: Moses “wondered at the sight” and drew near to look, and the voice of the Lord said, “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

God did not first assign a task; He first said who He is. Forty years earlier Moses thought God would deliver Israel “by his hand,” and then he knew many things but did not truly know God. Forty years later when God speaks, His first words are self-introduction. The order cannot be reversed: know God first, then be used by Him; get the relationship right first, then talk about service.

And God spoke as “the God of your fathers”—this God had not changed through four hundred years of silence; not one word He said to Abraham had been forgotten. Moses “trembled and dared not look.” At forty he dared to strike a man dead; at eighty he dared not lift his eyes—this is the change forty years of wilderness had made.
• Know Him first, then work for Him: don’t rush to ask “What should I do?”; first hear Him say “I am.”
• Reverence is the mark of maturity: the more a person knows God, the less casual he is; the less casual he is, the more God can entrust to him.
III. “The place where you stand is holy ground”—Holy Ground Is Not a Plot of Land, but Where God Is
Verse 33 is the center of this passage and the sharpest line of the sermon’s first main theme: “Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.”

What kind of ground was it? The wilderness of Sinai, sandy gravel trampled by sheep, overgrown with thorns. No temple, no altar, no priest, hundreds of miles from Jerusalem. Yet God said: this is holy ground. Why? Not because the ground was special, but because God was there. What makes ground holy is not the ground but God’s presence.

An ordinary hospital room has white walls and an iron bed, just like every other room; but because a mother lies in it, it becomes the most important place for the whole family, and everyone who enters walks softly. The room has not changed; who is there has changed it. The temple is like this, and so is the church—the building itself is not holy; it is holy because the Lord is in it; if the Lord is not there, the grandest temple is only stone. The council kept hold of the stones and pushed the Lord out.
• Wherever God is, that is holy ground: your office, your kitchen, your sickroom—wherever the Lord is, take off your sandals.
• Taking off sandals is returning to one’s place: sandals are a person’s own covering; taking them off admits, this is God’s place, and I am one standing before Him.
IV. “I have surely seen… I have come down to deliver them. Come now, I will send you”—God Sees, God Comes Down, God Sends
Verse 34 strings verbs together: I have seen, I have heard, I have come down, I will send you.

“Surely seen” is, in the original, “seeing, I have seen,” a repetition that is the Hebrew way of emphasis—I have truly seen. Israel had groaned in Egypt for four hundred years and may have thought God did not see; God says: I have seen, I have heard, not one day missed. Then He says, “I have come down”—not sending someone, but coming Himself. This was completely fulfilled on the night of the incarnation.

Only last comes “Come now, I will send you.” Forty years earlier Moses went on his own; forty years later God sent him. The same man, the same task; the only difference is who initiated it. Last time we spoke of “his hand” and “God’s hand”; here is the moment “God’s hand” is laid on him.
• God sees your distress: not one of your groans has escaped Him; His “coming down” simply has its own time.
• Go only when sent: deliverance is God’s work and we are the sent; it is not that I do it for God, but that God does it through me.
V. “The one the people rejected… God sent”—The Rejected One Became the Deliverer

Verse 35: Stephen says the same words from forty years ago, unchanged: “This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent to be both ruler and deliverer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.”

“Rejected” and “sent”—what man did and what God did are exact opposites. The man Israel pushed away, God made ruler; they asked “Who made you?” and God answers: I did. Verse 36 goes on: this very rejected man led the people out of Egypt, through the Red Sea, and through the wilderness, doing wonders and signs for forty years.

Hearing this, the council must have recalled what Peter said in the same place weeks earlier: “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). The same structure—man rejects, God exalts. Stephen is laying Moses and Jesus over each other: the way your fathers treated Moses is the way you treated Jesus.
• Man’s rejection cannot cancel God’s sending: if the one pushed away was sent by God, God Himself will put him back.
• This is also Jesus’ road: rejected by His own, yet the “deliverer” God appointed. Those who follow Him should not be surprised at being rejected.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Only Those Who Take Off Their Sandals Can Be Sent
What happened before the burning bush has a clear order: God appears → God says who He is → Moses takes off his sandals → God says “I will send you.”

The sandals come off in the middle. Sandals are a person’s own—his own qualifications, methods, plans, the hand that dared to strike forty years before. God had Moses take these off first, admitting this is His place and His work, and only then sent him. This is the order of relationships: first with God, then with self, then with people, then with tasks. Moses at forty skipped the first two steps and went straight to work, and was pushed away; Moses at eighty took off his sandals first, and then God entrusted Israel to him.

Letting Jesus be King, in concrete form, is taking off the sandals: standing before Him and admitting that this piece of ground, this matter, these people are all His, and I am only the one sent. And one God sends need not defend his own authority—the question “Who made you?” is answered by God Himself. A person emptied of self can be rejected in peace, because he knows who appointed him.
a: Wait for the Appearing in the Wilderness
Your most ordinary, least spiritual-feeling days may be the very bush where God means to speak.
First Hear Who He Is
In prayer today, ask for nothing at first; quietly listen to God say, “I am the God of your fathers.”
Treat the Ground Beneath You as Holy
Before you enter the office or the kitchen, take off your sandals in your heart.
Believe He Has Seen
Hand over again the thing you groan about, and believe He has “surely seen.”
Be Rejected in Peace
When someone asks “Who made you?”, don’t defend yourself; let God answer.
q: God said, “The place where you stand is holy ground.” If the Lord were in the most ordinary place you are going today, what would be different for you? Are you willing to “take off your sandals” before entering?
Moses was sent only at eighty. Is there something in your life you spoiled with your own hands at forty and that God may now be sending you to do again? This time, what will you do first?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You appeared to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and said from a bush, “This is holy ground.” Thank You for showing us that what makes ground holy is never the ground but Your presence; wherever You are is where we should take off our sandals. Thank You that You have surely seen the affliction of Your people, heard their groaning, and come down Yourself.
Lord, we confess that we often stand before You with our sandals on—carrying our own qualifications, methods and plans, rushing to work for You without first hearing who You are. Teach us to take off our sandals, to give Your place back to You and Your work back to You, and to be only those who are sent. Remove also our fear of being rejected, so that, like Moses, when we are pushed away we do not defend ourselves but trust the God who appointed us. May our offices, kitchens and sickrooms become holy ground by Your presence. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: This is that Moses, who said to the children of Israel, ‘The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me.’
This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel that spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living revelations to give to us,
to whom our fathers wouldn’t be obedient, but rejected him, and turned back in their hearts to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.’
They made a calf in those days, and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands.

But God turned, and gave them up to serve the army of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets, ‘Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?
You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan, the figures which you made to worship. I will carry you away beyond Babylon.’
b: In the last devotion, God appeared to Moses in the burning bush in the wilderness of Sinai, saying “the place where you stand is holy ground,” and sent this man whom the people had rejected to be ruler and deliverer. He led the people out of Egypt and through the Red Sea, and for forty years did wonders and signs.

Today Stephen finishes the story of Moses.
