The order of relationships is God first, then myself, then people, then tasks—Peter went up to the roof first, and then God connected the matter at Caesarea to him.
• Extra prayer: not a required hour but one he went up to on his own; God often speaks at such times.
• Go up to the roof first: God first, and then God brings people and tasks to me.
II. “He became hungry… he fell into a trance”—God Teaches Him Through His Hunger

Verses 10–12: while Peter prayed he became hungry, and downstairs a meal was being prepared. In this most ordinary of settings he “fell into a trance”—not asleep and dreaming, but brought into a vision while awake.

The sky opened, and a great sheet was let down by its four corners, “in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky.” This list was not random. Leviticus 11 divides animals into clean and unclean: animals that part the hoof and chew the cud may be eaten, the rest may not; most insects may not; many birds may not. This was a rule Jews recited from childhood, one of the marks that set them apart from Gentiles. Now, on one sheet, the clean and the unclean were mixed together and lowered before him.

God used Peter’s hunger as the teaching material, and while he was hungry set before him a table of things he would not eat. God’s favorite classroom is not a special meeting but our most ordinary needs—when we are hungry, tired, or lacking.
• The most ordinary classroom: God used the time of a meal to speak of something that would change history.
• A sheet with everything mixed together: God deliberately put together what Peter kept apart.
III. “Not so, Lord”—Calling Him Lord, Yet Telling Him “No”
Verses 13–14: the voice said, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!” Peter answered, “Not so, Lord, for I have never eaten anything that is common and unclean.”

There is a contradiction in that one sentence. He called Him “Lord,” yet told Him “Not so.” If He is Lord, how can there be a “Not so”? Yet that is how Peter answered—and his reason was “I have never.”

We should be fair to Peter. He had kept this rule all his life; this was not stubbornness but devotion. More sobering still, the Lord Jesus had already said, “all foods are clean” (Mark 7:19), and Peter had been present that time. He had heard the words but not taken them in, because they did not fit the habits of his whole life.

Every driver knows the experience: the navigation says, “Turn right ahead,” but we turn left every day, so the hands naturally steer left, and we even think the navigation is wrong. Peter’s “Not so” was like that—not that he did not love the Lord, but that his hands had grown used to turning left. The deepest hiding place of the self-life is not obvious sin but devotional habits of many years. It wears the cloak of “I have never,” so that when we say no to the Lord we still think we are keeping the rules.
• Lord and “not so” cannot coexist: if we call Him Lord, there is no room for “not so.”
• Self hides in habit: “I have never” is often self’s most devout sentence.
IV. “What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean”—Cleanness Is God’s to Decide
Verse 15: the second time, the voice said just one sentence: “What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.”

“Unclean” in the original is “common, ordinary”—what Jews used for things mixed in among the Gentiles and not set apart. “Cleansed” is a completed act: God has already cleansed it; not “you may regard it as clean.” Peter’s problem was not that he had a standard, but that his standard had stopped at a point God had already moved beyond.

The point of this sentence is not food. By verse 28 Peter himself unravels it: “God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.” The animals on the sheet were the textbook; the content of the textbook was people. What God wanted to tear down was the wall in Peter’s heart that divided people into “us” and “them.”

“The Bible is my standard”—Peter would have agreed with that completely. But the standard is God’s word, not a tradition I have built up out of God’s word. When tradition and God’s present word conflict, a person has to choose a side. To change from a human viewpoint to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly: this is the change Peter had to make there on the roof.
• Cleansing is God’s doing: it is not for me to judge who is clean, but to acknowledge whom He has already cleansed.
• The animals are the textbook, people the content: what God tears down is a wall, not table rules.
V. “This was done three times”—Three Times, Still the Same Peter; Three Times, Still the Same Lord
Verse 16: “This was done three times, and immediately the sheet was received up into heaven.”

Peter’s life is bound up with “three times”: three denials by the charcoal fire, three questions of “Do you love me?” by the sea, and now three times on the roof hearing “Rise, kill and eat.” He is still the same Peter—blurting out, saying “Not so” first, needing the Lord to repeat it three times before slowly turning. But He is also still the same Lord—never giving up, never angry; if once is not enough, then a second time and a third.

Notice one more thing: the sheet was taken back, but God gave no explanation. Peter came down from the roof with a head full of questions (verse 17 says he was “very perplexed”). God does not always finish the answer in the vision; He often places the answer in the next step—here, in the three men knocking at the door. Peter did not need to work it out on the roof; he only needed to go down and open the door.
• The patience of three times: we are slow, the Lord is not in a hurry; He says it again and again.
• The answer is at the door: what is left unfinished in the vision, God puts in the obedience of the next step.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Change Your Concepts, and You Change Your Life

At Cornelius’s end, God wanted obedience; at Peter’s end, God wanted a change of concepts. Neither is easy, but changing concepts is harder—because what needed to change was not a wrong thing but something he had believed was right all his life.

Change your concepts and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living; change begins with me. If Peter had not first been changed on the roof, when he went down to meet the three men he would have kept them outside the door according to the old rules. The door to a whole world hung on whether one man was willing to let God correct his concepts.

A life lived for self protects its own concepts, because concepts are the home it has built over many years; when God says “Rise, kill and eat,” its first reaction is “Not so.” A life emptied of self also has concepts and principles, but it hands the final verdict to God—what He says is clean, I no longer call common. Humility is not having no position; it is having a Lord above my position. What humility looks like today is that when God corrects me through His word and through brothers and sisters, I do not first say “I have never,” but first ask, “Lord, what do You want me to see?”
a: Go Up to the Roof
Beyond the set hours, give God an extra stretch of quiet; He often speaks there.
Listen While Hungry
God uses our most ordinary needs as His classroom; don’t miss it.
Examine Your “Not So”
When you have said “not so” to the Lord, was the reason “I have never”?
Acknowledge That He Has Cleansed
It is not for me to judge who is clean, but to acknowledge whom God has already accepted.
Come Downstairs with Your Questions
You don’t have to work it all out before moving; the answer is often in the obedience of the next step.
q: Think of a habit or practice of faith that you have assumed for many years was “of course so.” Have you asked the Lord whether it is His standard, or a tradition you built up from His standard?
God told Peter to go down with his questions and open the door. Is there something right now that you haven’t worked out, yet you already know the next step? Are you willing to take that step first?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You work at both ends at once, with the timing exact; that You used the time of a meal and one man’s hunger to speak of something that would change the whole world. Thank You for Your patience with Peter—once, twice, three times, never giving up and never angry.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we too often call You Lord with one breath and tell You “Not so” with the next; what we are least willing to let You touch is often not obvious sin but habits of many years and concepts we have believed right all our lives. Forgive us for treating our own traditions as Your standard. As You did with Peter, put together what we have kept apart, and let us see whom You have already cleansed and accepted. Holy Spirit, correct our concepts, so that our lives are changed and our daily living follows; and make us willing to go downstairs and open the door even with questions not yet worked out. May You be King over our concepts and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate,
and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there.
While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three  men seek you.
But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”
Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.”
So he called them in and provided a place to stay. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
b: In the last devotion, the sheet was taken back into heaven, but God gave Peter no explanation. He stood on the roof with his heart full of questions.

In this devotion the answer comes—not from heaven but from outside the gate. While he was still wondering what the vision meant, someone downstairs called his name. At this moment God connected the lines at both ends.
I. “While Peter was very perplexed… stood before the gate”—The Answer Is Not on the Roof but at the Door
Verses 17–18: Luke sets two things precisely side by side: Peter upstairs “perplexed,” and three men downstairs “standing before the gate.”

“Perplexed” is not doubting God; it is not being able to work it out. The rules he had kept all his life had been turned over by God three times, and he did not know what it meant. While he was thinking, the men sent by Cornelius “made inquiry for Simon’s house”—asking all the way until they found this tanner’s house by the sea—“and stood before the gate, and called and asked whether Simon, who was surnamed Peter, was lodging there.”

Anyone who does jigsaw puzzles knows that when a piece in your hand will not fit, the problem is not that piece; the other piece has not arrived yet. Peter had one piece in hand: the sheet, the animals, “what God has cleansed.” Looked at alone, it made no sense however he turned it. The other piece was at the gate calling his name. God often leads this way—first one piece we cannot understand, then another, and only together do the two make a picture. When we cannot work it out, we need not force our thinking; we can listen for a voice at the door.
• Perplexity is not unbelief: not working it out is normal; God’s picture is not finished yet.
• The other piece is at the door: a vision we cannot understand is often unlocked by someone’s knock.
II. “The Spirit said to him… doubting nothing, for I have sent them”—What the Spirit’s Leading Looks Like
Verses 19–20: while Peter was still thinking, “the Spirit said to him, ‘Behold, three men seek you. But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.’”

Notice the shape of this speech. The Spirit did not explain the vision; He gave just four actions: arise, get down, go with them, doubt nothing. The actions were clear, and the reason was one sentence: “for I have sent them.”

The phrase “doubting nothing” can also be translated “making no distinction” (see the margin note at Acts 11:12). This is exactly the key to the whole passage—what the Spirit said to Peter was not only “don’t doubt,” but “don’t sort people into categories.” Don’t see that they are Gentiles, that they are Roman soldiers, and file them under another class.

There is an even better line: “I have sent them.” It was plainly Cornelius who sent them, yet the Spirit says, I sent them. When God is at work, everything human hands do has Him behind it. This is what the Holy Spirit as my guide looks like in daily life: He seldom explains the whole picture to us; He usually says only the next step—arise, get down, go with them. As for why, we find out by going. To rely on the Spirit with the heart is to hear “get down” and get down; to rely on my own head is to stand upstairs and think through all the reasons before moving, and by then the men at the door are long gone.
• The Spirit gives actions, not the whole picture: arise, get down, go—walk first, understand later.
• Make no distinction: the men at the door are not “that kind”; they are those He sent.
III. “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”—Go Down First, Then Ask
Verse 21: Peter went down. He spoke two sentences: “Behold, I am he whom you seek. What is the reason why you have come?”

The first is an acknowledgment: I am he. He did not hide, did not have the tanner send them away, did not first ask for details before deciding whether to show himself. The second is a question: why have you come? He assumed no answer and let them speak.

These two sentences look ordinary, but only a man who had just been turned around could say them. If it had been Peter an hour earlier—the Peter who said, “Not so, Lord”—he would probably have stayed upstairs and asked for clarity first. Now he went down, stood before three Gentiles, handed himself over first, and then listened to what they wanted.

We often do it the other way around: we first ask who the other person is and what he wants, and then decide whether to go down. But people matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. Peter stood before the people first, and then there was something to talk about. The first step of obedience is often for the body to move first—go downstairs, open the door, stand before that person.
• Show yourself first: I am he; don’t hide upstairs and send people away.
• Ask first, assume nothing: why have you come? Let the other speak; don’t decide for him.
IV. “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, well respected by the whole nation of the Jews”—God Was Already at Work in Them

Verse 22: the three men spoke: “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well respected by the whole nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to hear words from you.”

They knew Peter was a Jew, so they made a point of saying that Cornelius was “well respected by the whole nation of the Jews”—he was no enemy; even the Jews spoke well of him. They also stated their purpose very clearly: not to ask Peter to do something but “to hear words from you.” What Cornelius wanted was not miracles or help but words.

When Peter heard this, the puzzle piece from the roof snapped into place. God had already prepared in Caesarea a man, a household, a group waiting to hear. Peter was not going to break new ground; he was going to reap what God had already prepared. We often think that evangelism is “I go to bring God to him”; more often, God is already there waiting, and only sends us to tell what He has already done. The focus is on Jesus, not on myself—it is not how well I can speak, but that He is already there.
• The other person has already been prepared: God first worked in Cornelius, and then sent Peter.
• Go and tell, not go and create: not bringing God there, but telling what He has already done.
V. “Peter called them in and lodged them… some of the brothers from Joppa went with him”—The First Step Across the Line, at His Own Front Door
Verse 23 has two actions, both inconspicuous and both important.

First, “Peter called them in and lodged them.” Three Gentiles, one of them a Roman soldier, were invited into a Jew’s house to stay the night. By the rules of that time, a Jew was not to associate with or visit a Gentile (verse 28). The first step of the gospel into the Gentile world was not in Caesarea but in Joppa—in the place where Peter himself was staying, beginning with inviting people in. Crossing the line is never first about going somewhere far away; it is first about opening the door at one’s own front door.

Second, “some of the brothers from Joppa went with him.” Later we learn there were six (Acts 11:12). Peter knew this would stir controversy, so he did not go alone. On one hand it was witness—when he returned to Jerusalem, six men could testify; on the other, it was the humility of one emptied of self—he did not take this unprecedented thing upon himself alone. What humility looks like here is: before doing a great thing, first find some brothers to go with you, so that you are not the only one who can speak.
• Begin at the front door: the first step across the line is inviting the person at the door to stay the night.
• Don’t go alone: take brothers along, so the witness does not rest on me alone.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Only the One Emptied of Self Can Be Led by the Spirit
In these seven verses the Spirit speaks only once, and what He says is: arise, get down, go with them, doubt nothing.

The Spirit’s leading is seldom long speeches; it is usually just these few words. The difficulty is not in failing to hear, but in whether we will move once we have heard. Peter could be led not because he was especially spiritual but because on the roof a wall had already been torn down in him—the sentence “I have never” had been interrupted three times, and his self had loosened. Once self loosened, when the Spirit said one word, “get down,” he got down.

A life lived for self also wants to be led, but it wants to see the reasons first, confirm the results first, sort the categories first. For such a person, the Spirit’s words keep getting stuck on “why” and cannot pass. A life emptied of self is not without questions—Peter was “perplexed” too—but it carries its questions and takes the step first: go downstairs, open the door, invite them in, go together tomorrow. When self-denial is no longer I but Christ, leading is no longer my hearing and then evaluating, but His saying and my going. God can use such a person to open the door to a whole world.
a: Don’t Force It; Listen at the Door
The answer to a vision you cannot understand often comes through someone’s knock.
Get Down When You Hear
The Spirit gives actions, not the whole picture; walk first, understand later.
Make No Distinction
The person at the door is not “that kind,” but one He sent.
Show Yourself, Then Ask
Stand before the person and let him speak; don’t decide for him.
Cross the Line at Your Front Door
Inviting someone in for the night is harder than going far away, and more real.
q: Is there a situation you cannot work out right now, where God’s other puzzle piece is already “at the door”—some person, some matter—and you are still upstairs forcing it?

“Make no distinction.” Is there a kind of person in your heart that the Spirit has told you to go to, yet you first sorted them into a category? What could the first step across the line be, today, at your own front door?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that when Peter could not work it out on the roof, You had already brought the answer to the door. Thank You that in Caesarea You had already prepared a man, a household, a group waiting to hear; in every place we go, You have arrived first.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often stand upstairs thinking through all the reasons before we will go down, and the people at the door are long gone; we also often sort people into categories first before deciding whether to open the door. Forgive us. Holy Spirit, say also to us, “Arise, get down, go with them, doubting nothing,” and give us a loosened heart that goes as soon as it hears. Teach us to begin crossing lines at our own front door—inviting in, lodging for the night, setting out together; and teach us not to go alone but to take brothers along in everything, and not take Your work upon ourselves. Be our guide, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.
When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him.
But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”
As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together.

He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.
Therefore I also came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”
Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,
and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God.
Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He is staying in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’
Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”
b: In the last devotion, Peter invited three Gentiles in to stay the night, and the next day set out with some of the brothers from Joppa. The gospel had crossed the boundary of the Jews, and the first step had already been taken at his own front door.

In this devotion the two ends finally meet. A Roman officer and a Jewish fisherman stand together in a house in Caesarea. Both had been prepared by God, and both would be corrected once more in this encounter.
I. “Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends”—Open the Home, Gather the People

Verse 24: “On the next day they entered into Caesarea.” After more than a day’s journey from Joppa, they had arrived. Cornelius was not waiting alone: he was “waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.”

He had sent for a Jew he had never met, not knowing whether he would come or what he would say, yet he did not wait for certainty but first gathered all his relatives and friends. Verse 27 says “many were assembled.” Cornelius’s faith was not “let me listen first, and if it’s good I’ll introduce it to others,” but “God said He has words for me, so let everyone I care about come and hear together.”

When a person receives something good, the most natural reaction is to hide it; when a person receives God’s word, the most natural reaction should be to open the home. Since verse 2, Cornelius’s house was a house that feared God with all its members, and now it became the house where the gospel first entered the Gentile world. God’s system does not begin with an organizational structure; it begins with one person willing to open his home.
• Invite people without waiting for certainty: God said He has words for me, so let those I care about hear together.
• The home is the first domain: God’s system often begins with an opened house.
II. “Stand up. I myself am also a man”—Not Accepting Glory That Does Not Belong to Him
Verses 25–26: as soon as Peter entered, Cornelius “met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him.” But Peter “raised him up, saying, ‘Stand up. I myself am also a man.’”

Cornelius was a centurion, a person of standing in Caesarea. He fell prostrate at the feet of a Jewish fisherman, an act of great reverence—in his mind, the man an angel had directed him to send for must be more than ordinary. But Peter immediately raised him up. “I myself am also a man”—literally, “I myself am only a man.”

A mail carrier delivers an important letter, and the recipient, overcome, bows down to the carrier. What would the carrier do? He would say: I am only the one who delivers; I did not write the letter. That is exactly how Peter was. The words he brought were the Lord’s; he himself was only the one who delivered them. Cornelius was worshiping the wrong object, and if Peter had accepted it, the focus of the whole encounter would have moved from Jesus to Peter.

Letting Jesus have all the glory has its most practical test right here: when people put glory on me, do I raise them up? A life lived for self enjoys it a little and then says something polite; a life emptied of self makes raising up the first move—stand up, I am also a man. This is also the most accurate definition of humility: lay down power and return to one’s place; let God be God and let people be people. Peter was not belittling himself; he was simply returning to where a man ought to stand.
• Raise them up: the moment someone puts glory on me, my first move is to raise, not to receive.
• I am also a man: not self-belittling, but returning to my place—the Lord wrote the letter; I only deliver it.
III. “It is unlawful, but God has shown me”—Telling Plainly of His Own Change

Verses 27–29: Peter went in, found many gathered, and his first words were a plain confession: “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation.”

This is not an easy sentence to say. In front of a houseful of Gentiles he admitted: by our rules, I should not have come. He did not pretend he had always been open-minded. Then he said, “but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.”

Notice this sentence. The vision on the roof was about animals; here Peter speaks of people—“any man.” He had read the lesson of the sheet rightly: what God showed him was not a table but people. And he told of his own change: this is how I used to think, and God corrected me. “Therefore I also came without complaint when I was sent for.”

Change your concepts and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living. Peter’s change was not an insight that stayed in his heart; it was more than a day’s walk, ending with him standing before a houseful of Gentiles. And he asked once more, “I ask therefore for what reason you sent for me?” He already knew roughly, yet still let them speak. This is a kind of respect—not rushing to talk, but listening first.
• Admit the old wall: I should not have come; don’t pretend I was always open.
• Read the lesson onto people: on the sheet were animals, but God was speaking of “any man.”
IV. “Four days ago, at this hour…”—A Testimony Without a Word Changed
Verses 30–32: Cornelius retold what had happened four days earlier: praying at the ninth hour, a man in bright clothing, the prayer heard, the gifts remembered, men sent to Joppa for Simon.

This was the third time Luke recorded this event (verses 3–6, verse 22, and here), and the content was consistent, with nothing added for effect. “Four days ago, at this hour”—even the time of day matched. A true thing is the same however many times it is told; an invented one grows with the telling.

Cornelius described the messenger as a man “in bright clothing”; unfamiliar with Jewish terms, he used honest words for what he had seen. He also once more put what God said at the center: your prayer has been heard. In the whole account there is not one sentence boasting of himself; it is all what God did. The shape of a person’s testimony shows where his focus is—on himself or on God.
• A testimony with nothing added: a true thing is the same however many times it is told; no need to make it bigger.
• The focus is on God: not one sentence boasts of self; it is all what He did.
V. “Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God, to hear all things that have been commanded you by the Lord”—The Best Congregation

Verse 33 is the loveliest sentence in this passage: “Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God, to hear all things that have been commanded you by the Lord.”

There are three things in this sentence. First, “I sent to you at once”—his obedience was swift. Second, “we are all here present in the sight of God”—he knew the main figure of this gathering was not Peter but God; the whole room had not come to see a celebrity but to be before God. Third, “to hear all things that have been commanded you by the Lord”—all things, not choosing what to hear; what the Lord commanded, not Peter’s own opinions.

This is the congregation every preacher longs to meet. They have not come to grade; they have opened their hearts completely and wait before God. Half the reason Peter’s message in the next devotion could go on until the Holy Spirit fell is here—the hearers were already prepared. Relying on the Spirit with the heart begins with listening to the message: not analyzing with the head whether the speaker is good, but receiving His word before God with the heart.
• In the sight of God: the main figure of the gathering is not the speaker but God.
• All things: don’t choose what to hear; whatever the Lord commanded, we want all of it.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Let People Be People, Let God Be God
In this passage two men are doing the same thing: putting themselves back in their place.

Cornelius fell down in worship, and Peter raised him up—“I am also a man.” Peter stood before the Gentiles, admitted the rules he had held, and then said, “God has shown me”—he was not the one who made the rules but the one who was corrected. And Cornelius said, “we are all here present in the sight of God, to hear all things that have been commanded you by the Lord”—the main figure was not Peter but the Lord. Both men were pulling the other, and pulling themselves, away from standing in God’s place.

Pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power, wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place—letting God be God and people be people. In today’s life it looks like this: when someone lifts me up, I turn the credit back to the Lord rather than politely accepting a few words of praise; when someone asks me for guidance, I speak the Lord’s word rather than packaging my own opinion as the Lord’s. The focus is on Jesus—Peter delivered the letter, Cornelius listened to the message, and neither was in the focus; in the focus was only that One. When He receives all the glory, the whole houseful of people will receive salvation.
a: Open Your Home
Don’t wait for certainty; first invite those you care about to hear God’s word together.
Raise People Up
The moment someone puts glory on you, your first move is to raise, not to receive.
Confess Your Own Wall
Admit I should not have come, and then tell how God corrected me.
Testify Without Adding
A true thing is the same however many times it is told; keep the focus on what He did.
Be the Best Listener
Before God, listen to all His words, not choosing, not grading.
q: The last time someone thanked or praised you, was your first move to “raise him up,” or did you enjoy it for a moment? At that moment, who was the focus on?
Cornelius gathered his relatives and close friends without waiting for certainty. Is there a group around you or in your home that you have “waited to listen to first” and so never invited?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting a Roman officer and a Jewish fisherman stand together in one house. Thank You for preparing the home Cornelius opened and the heart Peter had corrected; You worked at both ends, and now the two ends are joined.
Lord Jesus, we confess that when people put glory on us, we often accept it with a few polite words; we also often refuse to admit the walls we had in our hearts, pretending we were always open. Forgive us. Give us Peter’s action—to raise people up and say, “I am also a man”; and give us Cornelius’s heart—to send at once, to open the home, and to want to hear all Your words before You. Bring us back to our place, letting You be God and us be human; may every letter we deliver let people see that You are the one who wrote it, and may You receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism;
but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.
The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all—
you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached;
even Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree.
God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed,
not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead.
All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”
b: In the last devotion, Cornelius finished speaking: “Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God, to hear all things that have been commanded you by the Lord.” A houseful of people, hearts already open, waiting.

In this devotion Peter opens his mouth. This is the first sermon in Acts preached to Gentiles. He did not compose a different message for them; he preached the same Jesus of Nazareth: how He lived, how He died, how He rose, how He will judge, and how He now forgives sins. There is only one gospel; this time, the door was simply opened wider.
I. “Truly I perceive that God is no respecter of persons”—A Lesson Just Learned
Verses 34–35: Peter’s first sentence was: “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism.”

“I perceive” in the original is “I truly grasp”—the words of someone who has only just understood. Four days earlier, on the roof, he was still saying, “Not so, Lord”; today, standing before a houseful of Gentiles, he says: I see it now. “Doesn’t show favoritism” in the original is “doesn’t look at the face”—that is, God does not decide whether to accept someone by appearance, nationality, or status.

An emergency room does not check your ID before deciding whether to save you. Whoever is lying at the door is treated first. God’s house is like that: “In every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.” This does not mean one can be saved by working righteousness—Cornelius had worked righteousness for years and still needed to hear the gospel to be saved; it means that God does not shut a person out because he is a Gentile. “Acceptable” means “able to come before God.” The door is open, and people of every nation may enter.
Peter spoke out at once the lesson he had just learned. His preaching was powerful because he was not speaking doctrine but what God had done in him in those four days.
• I perceive: the most powerful preaching tells what God has just done in oneself.
• God does not look at the face: the door is open, and people of every nation may come before Him.
II. “Through Jesus Christ… preaching good news of peace”—He Is Lord of All, and He Is the Example
Verses 36–38: Peter came to the content of the gospel. God was “preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ,” and he added in passing, “He is Lord of all.”

“Peace” here has two layers: peace between people and God, and peace between Jews and Gentiles. Paul later put it more clearly: “He came and preached peace to you who were far off, and to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). And the One who preached peace is “Lord of all”—not only Lord of Israel, but of all. If He is Lord of all, Cornelius’s whole houseful of people are within His “all.”

Then Peter spoke of how Jesus was on earth: “how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good, and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.” This sentence condenses Jesus’ life into a few actions: anointed by the Spirit, went about, did good, healed people, God with Him. This is Jesus is my example—He is the Son of God, yet He did not act on His own; He came out only after being anointed by the Spirit; He did not sit in one place waiting for people to come; He went about; and what He did was not earth-shaking deeds but “doing good,” one act at a time.
• Lord of all: His lordship has no boundary, and this houseful of people is also within His “all.”
• What the example looks like: anointed by the Spirit, going out, doing good—one act at a time.
III. “We are witnesses… whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree”—Peter Does Not Hide the Cross
Verse 39: Peter said, “We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree.”

“Hanging on a tree” is a deliberate phrase. The law of Moses says, “he who is hanged is accursed of God” (Deuteronomy 21:23). By using this phrase, Peter is saying that Jesus did not die merely a cruel death but a cursed death—He bore the curse for people.

Before a houseful of Gentiles, Peter did not soften this part. He could have spoken only of miracles and good deeds; but he spoke of the tree. A gospel without the cross is left as only the story of a good man. There is pain in the word “also”—He did so much good, and yet they killed Him. The “they” here is the Jews, but Peter knew in his own heart that he too had once abandoned Him by the charcoal fire. No one can stand outside the cross and say, “They did that.”
• Don’t hide the tree: a gospel without the cross is left as only the story of a good man.
• No one stands outside: “they” killed Him, and I also once abandoned Him.
IV. “Who ate and drank with him”—The Resurrection Was Not Just Told; People Ate Meals Together

Verses 40–41: “God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed, not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.”

When Peter said this, he was standing in a home where a meal had been prepared. He said: we ate and drank with the risen Lord. This is the plainest evidence—ghosts do not eat, and hallucinations do not drink. By the Sea of Tiberias the Lord Himself grilled fish and bread for them (John 21:9–13); Peter was the very one who sat by the charcoal fire that day.

“Not to all the people”—God did not have the risen Lord appear publicly in the temple courts; He appeared only to chosen witnesses. God’s way has always been this: to entrust the truth to some people and then send those people to tell it. A witness is not a spectator; he is someone who will stake his whole life on that matter.
• Ate a meal together: the resurrection is not an abstract doctrine; people sat at the same table with Him.
• The burden of a witness: when the truth is entrusted to a few, those few must spend their lives telling it.
V. “The Judge of the living and the dead” and “everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name”—The Most Solemn, Followed by the Most Wide

Verses 42–43: the close of the sermon. Peter spoke of judgment first: “He commanded us to preach to the people, and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead.” Then he spoke of forgiveness: “To him all the prophets testify that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”

This is a very honest order. First, He is the Judge—no one can get around Him; then, everyone who believes in Him will receive forgiveness—no one is excluded. “The living and the dead” is everyone; “everyone who believes in him” is also everyone. Judgment speaks of His authority reaching everywhere; forgiveness speaks of His grace reaching everywhere.

The word “everyone” is the door this sermon opened for the Gentiles. What all the prophets testified was not “the Jews who believe in him” but “everyone who believes in him.” Cornelius’s whole houseful of people were inside that “everyone.” Peter did not need to say any more; the door was open—and in the next devotion we will see the Holy Spirit fall on that very sentence.
• Judgment and forgiveness side by side: His authority reaches everywhere, and so does His grace.
• One word, “everyone”: the door was opened on this word.
The Light of the 321 Principles: There Is Only One Gospel, but the Door Keeps Opening Wider

The sermon Peter preached to the Gentiles has exactly the same backbone as the one he preached to the Jews at Pentecost: Jesus’ life, the cross, the resurrection, the witnesses, forgiveness. He did not change the content for a new audience. What changed was not the gospel but the speaker—four days earlier he would not enter this house; today he stands here saying, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism.”

The Bible is my standard. The standard did not change: the prophets had long testified, “everyone who believes in him.” What changed was that Peter finally read that “everyone” rightly. A life lived for self, reading the Bible, unconsciously reads “everyone” as “people like us”; a life emptied of self lets God’s word stand just as it is, even when that means many years of one’s own concepts must be corrected.

The focus is on Jesus. In this sermon there is not one sentence about Peter himself—not his vision, not his struggle, not his breakthrough. He gave the whole sermon to Jesus: He was anointed, He went about, He was hung, He rose, He judges, He forgives. What letting Jesus have all the glory looks like in preaching is that after the sermon, people remember Him, not the speaker.
a: Tell What You Just Learned
The most powerful testimony is what God has done in you these past few days.
Follow the Example
Anointed by the Spirit, going out, doing good one act at a time.
Don’t Hide the Tree
When you share the gospel, don’t make the cross sound nicer.
Stake Your Life on It
What you testify to—is it something you are willing to spend your whole life telling?
Read That “Everyone” Rightly
Don’t read “everyone who believes in him” as “people like us.”
q: “Everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name.” Think honestly: does the “everyone” in your heart have a boundary? Is there a kind of person you do not really believe He would forgive?
In his whole sermon Peter did not speak one sentence about himself. Recall the last time you gave witness for the Lord: how much did you speak of yourself, and how much of Him?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are a God who does not look at the face, and people of every nation may come before You. Thank You for preaching the good news of peace through Jesus Christ—He is Lord of all, and we are all within His “all”; He was anointed by the Spirit, went about doing good, and left us an example.
Lord Jesus, You were hung on a tree and bore our curse; on the third day You rose and ate and drank with Your disciples; You will judge the living and the dead, yet You promised that everyone who believes in You will receive forgiveness through Your name. We confess that we often read “everyone” as “people like us” and open the door smaller than You opened it; we also confess that when we speak of You we often speak of ourselves more than of You. Forgive us. Teach us, like Peter, to tell honestly what You have just done in us, and to give the whole testimony to You; may people remember You when they finish listening, and may You receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word.
They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.
For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered,
“Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.”
He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.
b: In the last devotion, Peter’s sermon stopped on one sentence: “everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins through his name.” That word “everyone” opened the door.

In this devotion, once the door opened, God came in. Before Peter had finished speaking, the Holy Spirit fell. This is the second Pentecost in Acts—the first in Jerusalem, on Jews; this one in Caesarea, on Gentiles. God Himself answered the question by what He did: may Gentiles? He did not answer with words; He gave them the Holy Spirit directly.
I. “While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word”—God Interrupted the Sermon

Verse 44: “While Peter was still speaking these words”—the sermon was not yet finished when the Holy Spirit fell. Peter had given no invitation, laid on no hands, led no prayer, and had not yet baptized anyone. God could not wait.

This must be read in contrast. In chapter 8 the Samaritans believed and were baptized, yet the Spirit did not fall until Peter and John came down from Jerusalem and laid hands on them (Acts 8:14–17). That time God had the apostles personally receive the Samaritans, so that the church would not split in two. This time God did not even give Peter the chance to lay on hands—He wanted every Jewish believer present to see plainly: I did this, not Peter, and no one approved it.

“All those who heard the word”—not a few but the whole houseful, every one. They had not first been circumcised, not first kept the law, not first become Jews; they were only listening, and when they heard “everyone who believes in him,” they believed, and the Holy Spirit came.

At a concert, the host is still giving his opening remarks when the musician walks onstage and begins to play. The host has to stop. Peter was that interrupted host—and he did not mind in the least, because he knew that what everyone was waiting for was never him.
• God does not wait for approval: what He wants to do does not need to pass through anyone’s hands.
• Hear, believe, receive: without first becoming “people like us,” the Spirit came.
II. “The gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out on the Gentiles also,” and They Were Amazed—The Six Brothers’ Astonishment

Verses 45–46: “those of the circumcision who believed, as many as came with Peter”—the six brothers who had come from Joppa—“were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.”

The word “poured out” is the same word Peter used at Pentecost when he quoted Joel, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Acts 2:17). Luke deliberately uses the same word to tell us this is the same event. And the sign is the same: “they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God”—at Pentecost the disciples also spoke in tongues and told of “the mighty works of God” (Acts 2:11). What God gave the Gentiles was not one bit less, not one thing missing.

The six brothers “were amazed.” This word is not doubt; it is being so astonished one cannot speak. They were circumcised Jews who had believed all their lives that the Spirit was for Israel; now they saw with their own eyes the Spirit poured out on a group of uncircumcised Romans in exactly the same way as on themselves at first. What God did went beyond their frame—and God meant to go beyond that frame.

We too have our frames: that kind of person won’t believe, God won’t use someone with that background, that place won’t have revival. Sometimes God deliberately works outside our frame, and more visibly than inside it, so that we are “amazed”—so that our frame is torn down.
• The same word, the same event: what the Gentiles received was not one bit less than Pentecost.
• Amazement is the sound of a frame coming down: God works outside your frame to tear your frame down.
III. “Can any man forbid the water, that these should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?”—Who Can Hinder God
Verse 47: Peter asked a question: “Can any man forbid water, that these who have received the Holy Spirit as well as we should not be baptized?”

“As well as we”—these words are Peter’s conclusion. Not “nearly,” not “second-class,” but the same. Since God gave them the same as us, by what right do we hold them back in the matter of water? The word “forbid” is the same word the Ethiopian eunuch used in chapter 8, “What is keeping me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36). Luke uses it twice, and both times the answer is: nothing hinders, no one can forbid.

Baptism’s meaning here is clear: it is not a ticket to receiving the Spirit but an acknowledgment of what God has already done. A customs stamp does not give a person the right to enter; it acknowledges that he already has that right; if the one holding the stamp refuses to use it, he is blocking himself, not the person’s right. Peter understood this, so he asked, “Can any man forbid”—meaning, who dares stand in front of what God has already done and say no?

What humility looks like here is: whom God has already accepted, I do not add another checkpoint. A life lived for self likes to add a door of its own in front of God’s door—one more condition, one more layer of review, so that it keeps a little power of decision. A life emptied of self sees that God has already stamped it and stamps it too at once. To let God be God is not to play lord a second time over what He has already settled.
• As well as we: what God gives has no second class, and we should not make a second class either.
• Stamp, don’t add gates: those God has accepted, we do not put another door of our own before His.
IV. “He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days”—Baptized, and Then Staying Together

Verse 48: two things. “He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ”—the Gentiles’ first baptism, and in the name of Jesus Christ. From then on Cornelius’s household was no longer “God-fearing Gentiles” but disciples of Christ, the same as the three thousand in Jerusalem.

Then, “they asked him to stay some days.” This looks like a mere closing line, but it carries real weight. For Peter to stay meant that in a Gentile’s home he ate, slept, and lived daily life—which is exactly what he would be questioned about in the next chapter on returning to Jerusalem: “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them” (Acts 11:3).

Peter could have finished the ceremony and left. Baptism done, mission accomplished, hurry back to Joppa before people talk. But he stayed some days. If crossing the line goes only as far as the ceremony, the line is still there; only when it reaches eating together and living together is the line truly gone. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things—the gospel entering the Gentile world was not a job finished but a group of people becoming one family.
• In the name of Jesus Christ: they share one name and one Lord with us.
• Staying on: if crossing the line goes only to the ceremony, the line is still there; only at the table is it gone.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Sovereignty Belongs to God; People Can Only Follow

In these five verses God did three things: the Spirit fell, the gift was poured out, tongues magnified Him. People did two things: were amazed, and baptized. The order is clear—God first, people following.

This is the most basic shape of letting Jesus be King. To be King means: He decides, I acknowledge; He moves first, I follow. In Caesarea nothing was led by Peter—he was called, interrupted, and driven by God’s deeds to a conclusion. All he did was not to hinder.

A life lived for self cannot bear this passivity. It wants to lead, to review, to keep the last vote, so it always adds a door of its own to what God has already done. A life emptied of self is like those six brothers—seeing, being amazed, and then tearing down its own frame and acknowledging what God has done. Self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless: when Peter laid down his one vote, he saw God’s work across the whole Gentile world.

And all of this comes finally to one sentence: “magnifying God.” When that houseful of Gentiles first opened their mouths, what they said was not what they had received but that God is great. Letting Jesus have all the glory is a group of people just filled with the Spirit, and their first words are exactly this.
a: Let God Interrupt You
What He wants to do need not wait for you to finish or for your approval.
Be Amazed at His Work Outside Your Frame
He works where you think it impossible in order to tear down your frame.
Don’t Add Your Own Door
Those God has accepted, don’t put another checkpoint before His door.
Cross to the Table
Don’t finish the ceremony and leave; sit down, eat together, and stay a few days.
Let the First Word Be “God Is Great”
When grace comes, praise Him first; don’t first tally what you got.
q: Do you have a frame in your heart—“that kind of person won’t believe,” “that place won’t have revival”? If God worked outside that frame today, would you be amazed, or would you doubt?
Think of a person or matter God has clearly accepted, yet you are still setting conditions. What is that extra door of yours actually protecting? Can you take it down today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that before Peter finished speaking, You poured out the Holy Spirit. Thank You for letting us see that what You gave the Gentiles was not one bit less than what You gave the disciples at Pentecost; what You want to do needs no one’s approval.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often want to add a door of our own before the one You have opened, one more condition, one more layer of review, so that we keep a little power of decision; we also confess that when we cross lines we often go only as far as the ceremony and are unwilling to sit down and eat together. Forgive us. Give us the eyes of the six brothers—seeing You work outside our frame, being amazed, and tearing the frame down; and give us Peter’s obedience—seeing that You have already stamped it, stamping it at once, and hindering no more. Be King; You move first and we follow; and when we receive grace, may our first words be “God is great,” and may You receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God.
When Peter had come up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision contended with him,
saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!”
But Peter began, and explained to them in order, saying,
“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain container descending, like it was a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners. It came as far as me.
When I had looked intently at it, I considered, and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky.
I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat!’
But I said, ‘Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.’
But a voice answered me the second time out of heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.’
This was done three times, and all were drawn up again into heaven.
b: In the last devotion, the Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius’s household, and Peter baptized them and stayed some days. The matter at Caesarea ended in fullness.

In this devotion, Peter returns to Jerusalem, and what waits for him is not a welcome but questioning. God had done a great thing outside, and those at home first knit their brows. This is a scene that appears after almost every breakthrough—and how Peter faced it was as important as how he preached at Caesarea.
I. “The apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God”—The Rumor Arrives Before the Man
Verse 1: Peter had not yet returned, but the news had arrived first. “The apostles and the brothers who were in Judea” all heard.

Notice how Luke writes the news: “the Gentiles had also received the word of God.” This is the positive way of putting it—not “Peter went to Gentiles’ homes,” but “the Gentiles received the word of God.” Luke wants us to know that the substance of this was that God’s word had been received, a good thing. But when good news reaches home, those who hear do not all hear it as good.

Caesarea is less than sixty miles from Jerusalem. News changes shape on the road. Some heard “the gospel entered the Gentile world,” others heard “Peter broke the rules.” The same event, different ears. When we hear news about brothers and sisters, which kind do we take in?
• News changes shape: the same event is heard as different things by different ears.
• Look at the substance first: God’s word was received—that is the substance; the rest is detail.
II. “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them”—The Point of Contention Was the Table, Not Baptism
Verses 2–3: “Those who were of the circumcision contended with him.” Their accusation was a single sentence: “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them.”

See clearly what they did not ask. They did not ask, “Why did you baptize Gentiles?” They did not ask, “How could the Holy Spirit fall on them?” They asked about eating. In Jewish thinking, eating at the same table meant accepting the other as part of the same family; sitting at table with the uncircumcised was the same as declaring that the dividing line did not exist. They could grudgingly accept Gentiles believing, but they could not bear Gentiles sitting at the same table as themselves.

This is very real. The fiercest arguments in the church are often not over the greatest truths but over the most personal habits. Doctrine can be discussed; what happens at the table touches a person’s “self”—my rules, my comfort, the way I have always been.

Notice one more point: the one being questioned was Peter—the chief of the apostles, the one who preached at Pentecost, the one who raised the lame man at the Beautiful Gate. Even when such a man came back to the church, people still contended with him, and he still stood and answered. In God’s system no one is beyond accountability; at the same time, being questioned does not mean being wrong. What new thing God does will always first unsettle some people.
• The argument was over the table: the fiercest arguments are often not about truth but about habit.
• No one is beyond accountability: even Peter had to answer; being questioned does not mean being wrong.
III. “But Peter began, and explained to them in order”—Not Pressing with Authority, but Speaking with Facts
Verse 4: “But Peter began, and explained to them in order.”

“In order” means by sequence, from beginning to end, one thing at a time. Peter did not say, “I am an apostle; who are you to ask me?” He did not say, “Didn’t you see that the Holy Spirit fell?” He did not lose his temper. He started from the beginning.

A witness in court does not argue; he only states: that day I was here, I saw this, I heard that. Peter was like that. He did not press with his position; he persuaded with facts. Only a truly humble person can do this—humility is not being silent but laying down power and returning to one’s place; what it looks like here is: I could easily use my status to overrule you, but I choose to tell you one thing at a time and let you see for yourself what God did.

People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. Peter cared not only whether the matter was “right” but whether these brothers could see it together. If the matter is right but people have not followed, the church splits in two. He spent time explaining in order because he wanted to take people along, not leave them behind.
• Explain in order: don’t press, don’t argue, tell the facts one by one.
• Bring people to see together: being right is not enough; people must follow, or the church splits in two.
IV. “I was in the city of Joppa praying… this was done three times”—Telling His Own “Not So” Too

Verses 5–10: Peter retold the vision on the roof at Joppa. Luke had already written it in chapter 10, and here writes it again almost word for word—a rare practice in Scripture; Luke is telling us this is important enough to hear twice.

Peter’s retelling has some details. He said the sheet “came even to me,” and that he “looked intently”—he wanted everyone to know he saw clearly, not a vague impression from a daze. He quoted the voice exactly: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!” And he quoted his own answer exactly: “Not so, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.”

This is the most admirable line. Before a group questioning him, Peter told of the “Not so” he himself had said. He did not present himself as open-minded from the start; he said: I was just like you are now. This is the most powerful explanation—not that I am wiser than you, but that I once stood where you stand, and God pulled me over.

Then came the key line, which he also quoted without change: “What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.” This is the standard. In the end Peter persuaded not by his own experience but by God’s word—experience can be disputed, but no one can dispute what God has said. The Bible is my standard: when people disagree, bring the dispute back before what God has said.
• Tell your own “Not so”: I once stood where you stand, and God pulled me over.
• Bring the dispute back to God’s word: experience can be argued, but no one can argue what God has said.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Change Begins with Me, and I Also Accompany Others as They Change
Chapter 10 was about Peter himself being changed; chapter 11 is about Peter accompanying a group as they are changed. Both are change, and the second is often harder.

Change your concepts and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living; change begins with me—Peter had already walked that stretch. But when he came home, he found the brothers still where he had stood four days earlier. He had two roads: one was to press with authority, “I am an apostle, the Spirit has already fallen, be quiet”; the other was to explain in order, starting from the beginning, even telling his own “Not so,” bringing people over one by one. He chose the second.

This is what self-denial looks like in the church. A person living for self wins an argument and loses a group of brothers; a person emptied of self is not in a hurry to win; he would rather spend more time and let the other see for himself what God did. He does not guard his own face—he tells “I too said not so at first”; he does not rely on his position—he speaks with facts and God’s word. Only such people can build God’s system. A system is not built by someone pressing down on someone else but by a group letting Jesus be King together.
a: Hear News by the Substance First
God’s word being received is the substance; a rule being broken is detail.
Discern What the Argument Is About
What touches your “self” is often a habit at the table, not truth.
Accept Being Questioned
No one is beyond accountability; being questioned does not mean being wrong.
Explain in Order, Don’t Press
When you could overrule with your status, choose to tell the facts one by one.
Tell Your Own “Not So”
I once stood where you stand—this is more powerful than being clever.
q: The last time you disagreed with brothers or sisters, was the argument over truth, or did it touch your “habits at the table”? Did you bring the matter back before what God has said?

When you have the status and the reasons to overrule someone, will you choose to “explain in order”? Think of a specific person: how could you bring him along to see together, rather than leave him behind?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You did a great thing among the Gentiles and did not leave behind those at home who had not yet caught up. Thank You for giving Peter a heart that did not press down on people, so that he explained from the beginning, in order, even telling his own “Not so,” and brought the brothers over one by one.
Lord Jesus, we confess that when we hear news about brothers and sisters, we often first hear “he broke the rules” and seldom first hear “You did a new thing”; in arguments we are often in a hurry to win, pressing with our status and guarding our own face. Forgive us. Give us Peter’s humility—not losing our temper when questioned, starting from the beginning, bringing the dispute back before Your word; and give us Peter’s honesty—not presenting ourselves as open-minded from the start but willing to admit we too once said “Not so.” May we not only be changed by You ourselves but also be willing to spend time accompanying others as they are changed; be King among us, not by someone pressing down on someone else, but by our letting You be King together. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me.
The Spirit told me to go with them, without discriminating. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house.
He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house, and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa, and get Simon, who is called Peter,
who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.’
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning.
I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’
If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?”
When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!”
b: In the last devotion, Peter stood before the brothers who questioned him, explained in order, began with the vision on the roof at Joppa, and told even the “Not so” he himself had said.

In this devotion he finishes the story: the three men at the door, the Spirit’s command, Cornelius’s house, the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Lord’s word, and then a question—“Who was I, that I could withstand God?” When he finished, the houseful of arguers fell quiet, and when they spoke again, what they spoke was glory to God. From argument to glory, there was only one honest explanation in between.
I. “Behold, immediately three men stood… these six brothers also”—The Timing Fits, and the Witnesses Are Present
Verses 11–12: Peter continued: “Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where we were, having been sent from Caesarea to me.”

“Immediately”—the vision had just been taken back, and the men were at the door. Peter wanted the brothers to note the timing: I did not put two events together afterward; God placed the two events at the same moment. Then, “The Spirit told me to go with them, without discriminating.” The margin note in some Bibles says this phrase can also be translated “making no distinction”—do not sort people into categories. This is exactly what the brothers were doing at that moment, and Peter said the Spirit had already told me not to do so.

Then a weighty line: “These six brothers also accompanied me.” They were standing right there. By Jewish rule, a matter was established on the mouth of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); Peter had brought six, seven with himself. He had known such a day would come, so when he went to Caesarea he did not go alone.
• God-arranged timing: not something I put together afterward; He placed two events at the same moment.
• Six brothers present: finding people to go with you before doing a great thing is both wisdom and humility.
II. “Who will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your house”—All of This Was for Salvation
Verses 13–14: Peter retold Cornelius’s words: the angel said, “Send to Joppa, and get Simon, who is surnamed Peter, who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.”

This sentence did not appear in chapter 10; it is new information given here. The angel’s purpose was stated clearly: not to make Cornelius a better person but to have him “be saved.” Cornelius was already a devout man, giving to the people, praying always, yet the angel still said, you need to hear some words in order to be saved. A good person is not a person already saved; good people also need Jesus.

“You and all your house”—God’s salvation begins in a person’s home. From verse 2 of chapter 10 Cornelius was a man who feared God with all his household, and now his whole household was saved. When a person lets Jesus be King in himself, the first to see it is usually his home.
• Good people need to be saved too: devotion and good deeds cannot replace the words “by which you will be saved.”
• Begin at home: when a person lets Jesus be King, the first to see it is his home.
III. “I remembered the word of the Lord”—Experience Must Come Back Before the Lord’s Word

Verses 15–16: “As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning. I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’”

“As I began to speak”—Peter honestly said that before he had finished, the Spirit fell. “Even as on us at the beginning”—“at the beginning” is Pentecost. He set the Caesarea event beside Pentecost and said: it is the same thing.

Then comes an important line: “I remembered the word of the Lord.” Peter had experienced something shattering, and his first reaction was not “I feel this is God” but to remember what the Lord had said. The words the Lord spoke before His ascension (Acts 1:5), he remembered in that house in Caesarea. Experience is the photograph, the Lord’s word is the negative—however clear the photograph, it has to be checked against the negative to know whether it is real. Peter’s experience stood not because it was shattering enough but because the Lord had said it long before.

This is the Bible is my standard: not using experience to interpret the Bible, but using the Bible to interpret experience. Many disputes in the church arise because someone takes his own experience as the standard. Peter’s way was to bring the experience back before the Lord’s word and let the Lord’s word decide.
• It fell as I began to speak: not that I spoke well, but that He could not wait.
• Remember the Lord’s word: experience is the photograph, the Lord’s word the negative; only what matches the negative counts.
IV. “Who was I, that I could withstand God?”—A Gatekeeper’s Place
Verse 17: Peter’s conclusion: “If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?”

“Since God gave”—sovereignty is God’s. “The same as us”—no difference. Then the question: who was I? This was said by the chief of the apostles. He was plainly Peter, the one to whom the Lord Himself had given the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:19), yet he said: who was I, that I could withstand God?

However faithful a gatekeeper is, he cannot keep the owner of the house outside the door. Peter knew clearly that he was the gatekeeper, not the owner. He held the keys, but the one who decides who may enter is the Lord. A life lived for self, once it has the keys, slowly forgets that it is only a gatekeeper and begins to think the door is its own and that those who enter need its consent. Peter had not forgotten.

The word “withstand” is the same word as “forbid” in chapter 10, “Can any man forbid the water.” Peter asked once in Caesarea and asked again on returning to Jerusalem. This is the most accurate picture of humility—laying down power and returning to one’s place; letting God be God and people be people. What it looks like today: when God has plainly worked in a person, I no longer block him with my own standards, even when I hold that power.
• Who was I: the gatekeeper is not the owner; the keys are in my hand, but the door is His.
• Do not withstand: where God has plainly worked, the power in my hand must be laid down.
V. “They held their peace, and glorified God”—From Argument to Glory
Verse 18: “When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God, saying, ‘Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!’”

In verse 2 they were contending; in verse 18 they “held their peace.” What happened in between was only one person honestly telling what God had done. They fell quiet not because they were overpowered but because they saw. Then they spoke, and what they said was not “All right, Peter, you win” but “glorified God.” If an argument ends with glory to God, that argument was worth having.

Their conclusion was also exact: “God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life.” Repentance is granted by God—not that the Gentiles worked it out themselves, but that God gave grace so that they could repent. “To life”—not merely joining the church but passing from death to life. This group that had just been arguing over a table now saw life.
• Held their peace: quiet that is not being overpowered but seeing.
• Glorified God: if an argument ends with glory to God, it was a worthwhile argument.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Letting Jesus Have All the Glory Begins with “Who Was I?”
At the end of this passage a houseful of people “glorified God.” And what enabled them to glorify Him was Peter’s earlier sentence, “who was I?”

If Peter had said, “I am an apostle, and I judge this to be God’s work,” the brothers would at most have yielded to Peter, and the glory would have fallen on Peter. But he said, “Who was I, that I could withstand God?”—he shrank himself to a gatekeeper and magnified God as the only One who decides. When a person shrinks, God appears great; as soon as he stepped back to his place, the glory naturally went to God.

Letting Jesus have all the glory is not adding “glory to the Lord” at the end of a sermon, but continually asking “who was I?” throughout the whole process. A life lived for self, after each time God uses it, quietly keeps a little glory for itself—the vision I saw, the sermon I preached, the people I brought; a life emptied of self tells the whole thing as what God did: the vision He gave, the people He sent, the Spirit He poured out, the words He had spoken. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me—when such a person has finished speaking, the hearers hold their peace and only glorify God.
a: Take People Along
Before a great undertaking, find brothers to go with you, so that later someone can witness with you.
Admit Good People Need Salvation
Don’t take your devotion as proof you are already saved.
Check Against the Negative
With every experience, first ask, “What has the Lord said?”
Remember You Are a Gatekeeper
The keys are in your hand, but the door is His; where God has worked, don’t block it.
Let the Argument End in Glory
Don’t ask the other to yield to me, only that he see Him.
q: “Who was I, that I could withstand God?” Think of a “key” you hold now—a role, a power of decision. Have you unknowingly come to treat that door as your own?
After your most profound recent spiritual experience, did you go back to “remember the word of the Lord” and let the Bible interpret it, or did you let the experience decide for itself?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You placed two events at the same moment, put six brothers on the scene, put the Lord’s word in Peter’s heart, and brought an argument to its end in glory to You. Thank You for granting grace to the Gentiles, and also to us, so that we may repent unto life.
Lord Jesus, we confess that once we hold a few keys we often forget we are only gatekeepers and begin to think the door is our own; when we experience something, our first reaction is often “I feel” and seldom “the Lord has said”; and each time You use us we quietly keep a little glory for ourselves. Forgive us. Put Peter’s “who was I” into our hearts, so that we shrink and You appear great; so that we bring our experience back before Your word and let Your word decide; so that when we finish speaking, those who hear remember You. Be King in every one of our arguments, and may all the glory go to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: They therefore who were scattered abroad by the oppression that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only.
But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus.
The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.
The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch,
who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord.
For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord.
Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul.
When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
b: In the last devotion, the brothers in Jerusalem held their peace and glorified God: “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!” Cornelius’s household was the first door through which the gospel entered the Gentile world.

In this devotion Luke pulls the camera back to the scattering of the disciples after Stephen’s martyrdom in chapter 8. Then we followed Philip to Samaria, but another group went north, and went farther. They had no names and no visions; they simply spoke as they went. And the city they reached would become the base from which the gospel went out to the whole world.
I. “Those who were scattered abroad by the persecution that arose about Stephen”—Affliction Scatters the Seed Farther
Verse 19: “Those who were scattered abroad by the persecution that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch.”
